title: Subscription webhook reads current_period_start/end that the installed Stripe API version no longer returns on the top-level Subscription object → every real subscription sync writes Invalid Dates and the Prisma update throws
description: billing.service.ts:463-464 reads top-level fields: `currentPeriodStart: new Date(payload.current_period_start * 1000)` / `currentPeriodEnd: new Date(payload.current_period_end * 1000)`. StripeSubscriptionShape declares these as top-level (stripe-driver.ts:57-58). Installed SDK is stripe@22.2.0 with default API version '2026-05-27.dahlia' (node_modules/stripe/esm/apiVersion.js: `ApiVersion = '2026-05-27.dahlia'`) and the real driver pins NO apiVersion (`new Stripe(env.stripeApiKey, { typescript: true })`, stripe-real.driver.ts:31). In that SDK the top-level `Subscription` interface (esm/resources/Subscriptions.d.ts:89) has `items: ApiList<SubscriptionItem>` (line 195) but NO current_period_start/end property — those exist ONLY on `SubscriptionItem` (esm/resources/SubscriptionItems.d.ts:54 `current_period_end: number;`, line 58 `current_period_start: number;`). In Subscriptions.d.ts the names appear only in doc comments and list-query RangeQueryParam params (lines 2566-2572). I proved the runtime consequence: `undefined * 1000 === NaN`, `new Date(NaN)` is an Invalid Date, and serializing it throws `Invalid time value` (which is exactly what Prisma 7.8.0 does when building the query for the DateTime? columns currentPeriodStart/currentPeriodEnd at schema.prisma:457-458). The webhook catch (stripe-webhook.controller.ts:105-117) then logs, stamps the error row, and drops the Redis lock.
impact: Every customer.subscription.created and customer.subscription.updated webhook throws at the subscription.update call, so new paid signups never flip planId/status/stripeSubscriptionId/cancel_at_period_end to the Stripe truth, and portal cancellations/resumptions never reflect locally. Stripe retries for ~3 days and the local stripe-retry sweep retries each tick — all failing identically — leaving paid tenants permanently desynced. Fully masked in CI: the webhook spec stubs BillingService (stripe-webhook.controller.spec.ts:44-51) and no spec builds a realistic dahlia payload (grep for current_period_start across apps/api/src returns only the buggy lines + the stale shape, never a test).
fix: Read the period from the subscription item: `payload.items.data[0]?.current_period_start` / `...current_period_end`, move those fields onto items.data[] in StripeSubscriptionShape, and guard against missing values (skip/null rather than building Invalid Dates). Add an integration test that feeds syncStripeSubscription a real dahlia-shaped payload. Pin an explicit apiVersion in the Stripe constructor so a future SDK bump can't silently shift the shape again.
skepticReasoning:
I tried hard to refute this and could not. Every link in the chain is verified against the real installed code, not types-on-paper.

1) Installed SDK: node_modules/.pnpm/stripe@22.2.0_@types+node@25.9.1/node_modules/stripe/package.json -> "version": "22.2.0". Its pinned default API version is `2026-05-27.dahlia` (esm/apiVersion.js and cjs/apiVersion.js both `ApiVersion = '2026-05-27.dahlia'`).

2) No api_version pin anywhere. stripe-real.driver.ts:31 is `new Stripe(env.stripeApiKey, { typescript: true })` — no apiVersion. A repo-wide grep for api_version/apiVersion in apps/api/src + packages returns nothing, and the app never creates webhook endpoints programmatically, so the webhook payload shape is whatever the account/endpoint API version is (basil/dahlia for any current account).

3) The fields are genuinely gone at RUNTIME, not just in the .d.ts. Stripe's own CHANGELOG.md in the installed package states at line 779 "Remove support for `current_period_end` and `current_period_start` on `Subscription`" and line 835 "Add support for `current_period_end` and `current_period_start` on `SubscriptionItem`", landing in API version `2025-03-31.basil` (CHANGELOG line 752). Confirmed in the type defs: in Subscriptions.d.ts the only real property declarations matching current_period_(start|end) are at lines 2568/2572 inside SubscriptionListParams (list range filters); the `Subscription` interface (line 89) carries only `items: ApiList<SubscriptionItem>` (line 195), no top-level period. SubscriptionItems.d.ts:54/58 declare `current_period_end: number;` / `current_period_start: number;` as the real home.

4) The buggy read: billing.service.ts:463-464 reads top-level `payload.current_period_start/end`. StripeSubscriptionShape (stripe-driver.ts:57-58) still declares them top-level and the controller casts with `as unknown as StripeSubscriptionShape`, so TypeScript never catches the mismatch. At runtime `payload.current_period_start` is undefined -> `undefined * 1000 === NaN` -> `new Date(NaN)` is an Invalid Date (verified: `new Date(undefined*1000)` is Invalid Date, isNaN true).

5) Prisma 7.8.0 (node_modules/.pnpm/@prisma+client@7.8.0...) THROWS on an Invalid Date for a DateTime field — verified in the actual runtime serializer (runtime/client.js): `if(Me(e)){if(Kt(e))return{$type:"DateTime",value:e.toISOString()};t.throwValidationError({kind:"InvalidArgumentValue",...underlyingError:"Provided Date object...})`, where `Me(e)` = `e instanceof Date` and `Kt(e)` = `e.toString()!=="Invalid Date"`. So a Date instance that is invalid takes the throw branch -> PrismaClientValidationError, during query building, before any DB round-trip. The target columns currentPeriodStart/currentPeriodEnd are DateTime? (schema.prisma:458-459). The update at billing.service.ts:456-474 therefore throws.

6) No internal try/catch in syncStripeSubscription (lines 424-483 contain no try/catch; only a comment with the word "retry"). The throw propagates to the controller catch (stripe-webhook.controller.ts:105-117): logs, stamps the error row, drops the Redis lock so Stripe retries.

7) Permanent desync + retry storm: the retry sweeper re-runs the identical path on the stored payloadJson (stripe-retry.job.ts:88-93 -> syncStripeSubscription) and fails identically every tick (stillFailing++), re-stamping the error until 30-day retention deletes the row.

8) CI masking confirmed: the webhook controller spec stubs BillingService entirely (stripe-webhook.controller.spec.ts: syncStripeSubscription: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined)). The only current_period_* references in apps/api/src are the two buggy lines + the stale shape (stripe-driver.ts:57-58); no test builds a realistic basil/dahlia payload.

Scope check: the bug affects customer.subscription.created and .updated only (both dispatch to syncStripeSubscription). customer.subscription.deleted is unaffected — handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted sets currentPeriodStart/End to null (billing.service.ts:504-505) and never reads the missing fields. That matches the finding exactly.

Caveat I checked and dismissed: the only way this would NOT fire is if a tenant's Stripe webhook endpoint were pinned to a pre-basil API version (< 2025-03-31). The code does not pin one and basil shipped over a year before the current date, so the realistic production configuration is broken. Severity critical is justified: every real paid signup/cancel/resume fails to sync, leaving paid tenants permanently desynced from Stripe truth (planId/status/cancelAtPeriodEnd never updated), i.e. billing-state corruption + money/access errors.
exploit:
Repro (no attacker needed — normal billing flow):
1. Deploy with STRIPE_DRIVER=real and stripe@22.2.0 (default API version 2026-05-27.dahlia, no api_version pin in stripe-real.driver.ts:31). Webhook endpoint on the current API version.
2. A tenant completes Stripe Checkout. Stripe sends customer.subscription.created. Its JSON has NO top-level current_period_start/current_period_end (those now live under items.data[0]).
3. Controller dispatch -> syncStripeSubscription(payload). billing.service.ts:463 computes `new Date(payload.current_period_start * 1000)` = `new Date(undefined*1000)` = `new Date(NaN)` = Invalid Date; same for :464.
4. controlDb.subscription.update (billing.service.ts:456) passes the Invalid Date to DateTime? columns. Prisma 7.8.0's serializer hits the `Me(e) && !Kt(e)` branch and throws PrismaClientValidationError ("Provided Date object is invalid") at query-build time.
5. The throw reaches stripe-webhook.controller.ts:105-117: error logged, error stamped on stripe_webhook_events row, Redis lock deleted. The local subscription row never flips planId/status/stripeSubscriptionId/cancelAtPeriodEnd to the Stripe truth.
6. Stripe retries for ~3 days and the local sweep (stripe-retry.job.ts:88-93) retries each tick — all failing identically — until 30-day retention removes the row. Result: paid tenant permanently on the stale (e.g. Starter/past_due) state despite a live paid Stripe subscription; portal cancels/resumes likewise never reflected.

Minimal proof points executed: `new Date(undefined*1000)` -> Invalid Date (isNaN true); Prisma runtime branch `if(Me(e)){if(Kt(e))...else throwValidationError}` with Me=isDate, Kt=valid-date; Stripe CHANGELOG lines 779/835 confirming the runtime field move.

Proposed fix is correct: read items.data[0]?.current_period_start/end, relocate those fields onto items.data[] in StripeSubscriptionShape, guard missing values (write null instead of Invalid Date), pin an explicit apiVersion in the Stripe constructor, and add an integration test feeding syncStripeSubscription a real dahlia-shaped payload.

title: tenant-relocate --drop-source drops the LIVE (destination) database, not the source
description: Cutover updates the live row to the NEW host: tenant-relocate.ts:136-139 `tx.tenant.update({ where: { id: tenant.id }, data: { dbUrl: newDbUrl, cellId: newCellId } })`. The only persisted copy of the OLD url is the audit event's beforeJson (line 147) which dropSource never reads. dropSource then derives everything from the now-updated row: line 173 `const sourceUrl = tenant.dbUrl;`, line 176 `const dbName = dbNameForTenant(tenant.id);`, lines 180-181 `const u = new URL(sourceUrl); u.pathname = '/postgres';`, line 189 `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS "${dbName}"`. The per-tenant DB name is deterministic from tenant id only (cli.ts:67-69 `return tenant_${tenantId...}`), so `tenant_<id>` is identical on every host. Thus --drop-source connects to the NEW host (now in tenant.dbUrl) and drops the live tenant DB there. Grep confirms no `from-db-url`/`previousDbUrl`/`oldDbUrl`/relocation-record exists anywhere to drop instead. The doc comment (lines 171-172 'we expect tenants.db_url to already point at the NEW home') and usage (lines 35, 159) explicitly instruct running --drop-source post-cutover.
impact: Running the documented post-cutover cleanup `pnpm tenant:relocate -- --tenant=acme --drop-source` permanently drops the just-migrated, now-live tenant database when source and destination are on different hosts — losing the library's entire catalogue, members, loans and circulation history. Only the degenerate same-host case (where source==destination host) happens to coincide and is safe.
fix: Persist the pre-cutover dbUrl (e.g. a relocation record or a required --from-db-url arg) and have --drop-source drop on THAT host. Add a guard that refuses to drop if `new URL(sourceUrl).host` equals the host now recorded as live in tenants.db_url. The audit beforeJson at line 147 already records the old URL and could be read as the source of truth.
skepticReasoning:
Confirmed after attempting refutation. Every load-bearing claim checks out against the real code.

1. Cutover overwrites the single source of truth. scripts/tenant-relocate.ts:135-139 updates the live row's dbUrl to the NEW host: `tx.tenant.update({ where: { id: tenant.id }, data: { dbUrl: newDbUrl, cellId: newCellId } })`. The Tenant model (packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:230) has exactly one `dbUrl` column and no previous/source-url field, so the old URL is gone from the row. The only persisted copy is the audit beforeJson at tenant-relocate.ts:147, and dropSource never reads auditEvent (verified by grep: auditEvent/beforeJson appear only at the write site, never in dropSource lines 170-195).

2. dropSource derives the target host from the now-updated row. tenant-relocate.ts:69-72 re-reads the tenant fresh; line 173 `const sourceUrl = tenant.dbUrl` is therefore the NEW host. Lines 180-182 open an admin connection to that host (path swapped to /postgres), line 186 terminates backends, line 189 `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS "${dbName}"`.

3. The DB name is host-independent. scripts/_lib/cli.ts:67-69 `dbNameForTenant` derives `tenant_<id>` from the tenant id alone — no host component — so `tenant_<id>` is identical on every host. Combined with (2), the drop lands on the NEW host's live DB.

4. No host guard exists. The only check in dropSource is tenant-relocate.ts:177 `/^tenant_[a-z0-9_]+$/.test(dbName)`, a name-format check; it never compares the connection host to the live host. There is no --from-db-url / previousDbUrl / relocation record anywhere (grep returned nothing).

5. This is the DOCUMENTED workflow. README.md:1991-1998 shows cutover to a different host (cell-02.lan) followed by `pnpm tenant:relocate -- --tenant=acme --drop-source`; README.md:2032-2034 and the script header (lines 20-35, 159, 171-172) explicitly instruct running --drop-source post-cutover to delete the old DB.

Refutations attempted and failed:
- Could --drop-source receive the source host another way? No. tenant-relocate.ts:75-77 short-circuits into dropSource before any cutover/arg-parsing of --to-db-url; --drop-source takes no host argument and ignores --to-db-url.
- Is the "same-host degenerate case" a meaningful safe path? No — it's stronger than the finding states. Because dbName is identical on both hosts, a same-host relocation yields newDbUrl === tenant.dbUrl, which is rejected at lines 87-88 ("destination URL equals current URL; nothing to do"). So every relocation that actually runs is cross-host, meaning EVERY documented --drop-source run targets the live DB. There is no safe coincidence in practice.

Consequence: running the documented post-cutover cleanup permanently DROPs the just-migrated, now-live tenant database (catalogue, members, loans, circulation history) while leaving the truly-stale source DB on the old host untouched. Total per-tenant data loss. Severity critical stands.
exploit:
Reproduce the documented cell-to-cell relocation:

1. Tenant `acme` (id `cmpp123`) lives on cell-01: tenants.db_url = `postgresql://lib:pw@cell-01.lan:5432/tenant_cmpp123`.
2. Run cutover: `pnpm tenant:relocate -- --tenant=acme --to-db-url='postgresql://lib:pw@cell-02.lan:5432/' --to-cell=cell-02`. The TX at tenant-relocate.ts:136-139 sets tenants.db_url = `postgresql://lib:pw@cell-02.lan:5432/tenant_cmpp123` (NEW host). The old DB still lives, intact, on cell-01.
3. Operator probes the new home (healthy), then runs the documented cleanup: `pnpm tenant:relocate -- --tenant=acme --drop-source`.
   - dropSource reads sourceUrl = tenant.dbUrl = the cell-02 URL (line 173).
   - dbName = dbNameForTenant('cmpp123') = `tenant_cmpp123` (cli.ts:67-69, host-independent).
   - Opens admin connection to cell-02.lan/postgres (lines 180-182).
   - Terminates all backends on tenant_cmpp123 on cell-02 (line 186) and `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS "tenant_cmpp123"` on cell-02 (line 189).
   Result: the LIVE, just-migrated database on cell-02 is destroyed; the stale source on cell-01 survives. acme loses its entire catalogue, members, loans and circulation history.

No mitigation exists: the name regex (line 177) passes for `tenant_cmpp123`, there is no host comparison, and the pre-cutover URL is recoverable only from auditEvent.beforeJson (line 147), which dropSource never reads.

title: --drop-source drops the freshly-relocated DB on the NEW host, not the old source
description: main() updates db_url to newDbUrl inside the control tx: scripts/tenant-relocate.ts:136-138 `await tx.tenant.update({ where: { id: tenant.id }, data: { dbUrl: newDbUrl, cellId: newCellId } });`. dropSource() then reads `const sourceUrl = tenant.dbUrl;` (line 173) and connects to `new URL(sourceUrl)` (line 180), pointing pathname at /postgres (line 181), and runs `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS "${dbName}"` (line 189). dbName = dbNameForTenant(tenant.id) (line 176), and dbNameForTenant only derives from tenant.id with no host component (scripts/_lib/cli.ts:67-69: `return \`tenant_${tenantId.replace(...).toLowerCase()}\`;`). So `tenant_<id>` exists with the same name on both source and destination hosts, and after a relocate tenant.dbUrl already points at the NEW host (the comment at lines 171-172 explicitly says so). The old source dbUrl is persisted ONLY in the audit event beforeJson (line 147 `beforeJson: { dbUrl: tenant.dbUrl, cellId: tenant.cellId }`), which dropSource never reads.
impact: Running the documented post-cutover cleanup `pnpm tenant:relocate -- --tenant=acme --drop-source` connects to the NEW host and drops the tenant's live production database that was just migrated there. The control plane still points db_url at that now-deleted DB; the tenant is fully down with total data loss, recoverable only from a backup that (per ops-dr-4/5) may not contain the relocated DB and has no tested restore path.
fix: Do not trust the current tenant.dbUrl in dropSource. Add an explicit `--from-db-url=` argument (or persist a previousDbUrl column / read the most-recent tenant.relocated audit beforeJson.dbUrl) and drop on THAT host. Add a guard that refuses to drop when the derived host equals the current tenant.dbUrl host. Until fixed, remove --drop-source from the docstring (lines 21, 34-35) and require a manual DROP with the source URL supplied by the operator.

title: read_only window not enforced for up to 30s after open; pg_dump starts immediately → writes lost on cutover
description: openReadOnly() writes the SystemModeEvent row directly (scripts/tenant-relocate.ts:201-210) — it does NOT call SystemModeService.openTenant(), which is the only path that busts the cache (apps/api/src/system-mode/system-mode.service.ts:122 `await this.bust({ tenantId: input.tenantId });`). The cache key is `system_mode:tenant:<id>` (system-mode.service.ts:27 `KEY_TENANT = (tenantId) => \`system_mode:tenant:${tenantId}\``), stored with TTL 30s (line 25 `const CACHE_TTL_SEC = 30;`, line 243 `set(..., 'EX', CACHE_TTL_SEC)`) under the lbr: prefix (RedisService keyPrefix 'lbr:', redis.service.ts:30). resolveTenant returns the cached value first (system-mode.service.ts:56-57). The middleware enforces read_only at read time and 503s mutations (system-mode.middleware.ts:123-129). The relocate script's bustResolverCache only deletes `tenant:slug:` / `tenant:sub:` (scripts/tenant-relocate.ts:277-278), NEVER `system_mode:tenant:<id>`. And main() calls openReadOnly at line 105 then pg_dump immediately at line 112-119 with no sleep — so any API process whose resolveTenant is cached NORMAL keeps accepting POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE for up to 30s while pg_dump's snapshot is already taken.
impact: Member/loan/catalog writes committed on the source in the ~30s after the read_only row is inserted (and during the dump window) are excluded from pg_dump's consistent snapshot and silently discarded when db_url flips to the new copy on cutover. The docstring's claim that read_only gives in-flight mutations 'a clean 503' (lines 6-8) is false for up to 30s. Silent partial data loss on every relocation under write load.
fix: After openReadOnly(), DEL lbr:system_mode:tenant:<id> using the script's Redis client (matching SystemModeService.bust), then sleep >= CACHE_TTL_SEC (30s, ideally with margin) before pg_dump so every API process observes read_only before the snapshot. Ideally check pg_stat_activity for non-idle backends on the source first. Same fix applies to scripts/storage-migrate.ts:88-96.

title: Signup endpoint provisions a Postgres database per request with no rate limit — resource-exhaustion DoS
description: auth.controller.ts:48-52 `@Post('signup')` with no `@UseGuards` (only complete-setup/me carry AuthGuard) → fully public. app.module.ts:73-78 registers ONLY `SupportAuditInterceptor` as a global provider — no `APP_GUARD`/ThrottlerGuard. `grep throttler` over apps/api returns nothing except the bespoke support-key limiter; package.json has no `@nestjs/throttler`. Caddyfile has no `rate_limit` directive (line 141 is only a comment). signup.service.ts:85 `placement = await this.provisioner.provision(...)`; tenant-provisioning.service.ts:126 `await admin.query(\`CREATE DATABASE "${dbName}" ENCODING 'UTF8'\`)` on the shared `pgSuperuserUrl`, then :135-138 four `CREATE EXTENSION` calls, then applyTenantMigrations :150 `execFileP('pnpm', ['exec','prisma','migrate','deploy'], {cwd: DB_TENANT_DIR ...})` spawns a child process per signup, then seedDefaults opens another Prisma client. The only pre-flight gate is signup.service.ts:56 slug-uniqueness, trivially bypassed by varying the slug.
impact: An attacker scripting POST /auth/signup with unique slugs creates unbounded physical Postgres databases on the shared cell, plus a `prisma migrate deploy` child process per request. Exhausts Postgres connections/disk and CPU/memory from piled-up child processes, degrading or crashing the shared Postgres that ALL tenants depend on, and pollutes the control plane with junk Tenant/User/Subscription/BillingAccount rows.
fix: Add a strict per-IP rate limit (e.g. a few/IP/hour) plus a global signup cap via @nestjs/throttler backed by Redis, gate behind Turnstile/CAPTCHA (none exists), and fix the trust-proxy/X-Real-IP issue (ratelimit-5) first so the per-IP key is the real client. Consider a bounded provisioning concurrency queue so even a burst can't spawn unbounded `prisma migrate deploy` processes.

title: Admin lockout is permanent — status set to 'locked' but never restored to 'active', bricking the account
description: Failure branch writes `status: locked ? 'locked' : admin.status` (admin-auth.service.ts:69). Success branch resets only counters: `data: { failedAttempts: 0, lockedUntil: null, lastLoginAt: new Date() }` (lines 75-78) — it never touches `status`. AdminAuthGuard rejects every request where status is not active: `if (!admin || admin.disabledAt || admin.status !== 'active') throw new ForbiddenException(...)` (admin-auth.guard.ts:30). A repo-wide grep for adminUser.update/updateMany returns only admin-auth.service.ts (the 'locked' writer) and mfa.controller.ts (MFA enrollment, never sets status). No admin-users management controller exists. Schema comment confirms intent was transient: `locked // temporarily locked due to too many failed redemptions` (schema.prisma:61).
impact: Any platform admin who enters a wrong password MAX_FAILED_LOGINS (default 5) times is permanently locked out of the entire /admin/* surface, including the support-key redemption console, with no self-service recovery — fix requires a manual DB UPDATE. An attacker who knows an admin's email can deliberately brick the console by spraying 5 wrong passwords. Note: only a *real* admin email can be locked (unknown emails return early via dummyVerify at lines 45-50), so the DoS is targeted but precise.
fix: On successful verify() reset status too: `status: admin.status === 'locked' ? 'active' : admin.status`, or stop overloading `status` for transient lockout and rely solely on `lockedUntil` (mirroring the tenant LoginService, which never mutates status).
skepticReasoning:
CONFIRMED. Every line in the finding checks out, and the failure path is worse than described.

Mechanics (verified by reading the code):
- On the Nth wrong password (N = env.maxFailedLogins, default 5 per apps/api/src/config/env.ts:201), the failure branch writes `status: locked ? 'locked' : admin.status` (apps/api/src/admin/admin-auth.service.ts:69), persisting `status='locked'` to admin_users.
- The success branch writes only `{ failedAttempts: 0, lockedUntil: null, lastLoginAt }` (admin-auth.service.ts:75-78). It never touches `status`. By contrast the tenant LoginService.recordFailure (apps/api/src/auth/login.service.ts:160-177) is purely time-based — it sets only failedLogins/lockedUntil and never mutates status — proving 'locked' status mutation was not the intended lockout mechanism. The schema comment AdminStatus { locked // temporarily locked... } (packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:61) confirms 'locked' was meant to be transient.
- AdminAuthGuard.canActivate rejects every /admin/* request where `admin.disabledAt || admin.status !== 'active'` (apps/api/src/admin/admin-auth.guard.ts:30). status='locked' fails this permanently.

No in-app recovery exists. A repo-wide grep for adminUser.update/updateMany returns exactly two app writers: admin-auth.service.ts (the 'locked' writer) and apps/api/src/support/mfa.controller.ts:79-87 (writes only mfaSecretCipher/mfaNonce/mfaKeyId/mfaEnabled — confirmed, never status). The admin module contains no admin-users management controller (only admin-auth, admin-overrides, admin-plans, admin-tenants, fleet). The ONLY thing that restores status:'active' is the out-of-band CLI scripts/bootstrap-admin.ts:58-69, which requires DB/server access and also force-resets the password — not self-service recovery.

The chain is actually subtler/worse than the finding stated: verify() only rejects on status==='disabled' (admin-auth.service.ts:51) and on a live lockedUntil (line 54) — NOT on status==='locked'. POST /admin/auth/login is unguarded (apps/api/src/admin/admin-auth.controller.ts:33). So once the 15-min lockedUntil window (default LOGIN_LOCKOUT_MS) elapses, the admin CAN log in with the correct password: verify() succeeds, the success branch clears lockedUntil but leaves status='locked', and the controller issues a valid session cookie (HTTP 200). Yet every subsequent guarded route — GET /admin/auth/me (admin-auth.controller.ts:47) and the whole support/fleet/tenants/overrides surface — returns 403 'Your admin account is no longer active.' The admin is in a baffling state where login looks successful but nothing works, with zero self-service exit.

Targeted-DoS premise also holds: unknown emails early-return via dummyVerify (admin-auth.service.ts:45-50), so only a real admin email can be locked, but for a known admin email the brick is reliable and precise. There is NO rate limiting in front of admin login — the only throttler in the codebase (support-rate-limit.ts) is wired solely into the support-key redemption endpoint (admin-support.controller.ts:90), not into /admin/auth/login. So 5 unauthenticated POSTs with wrong passwords permanently brick a chosen admin's entire console, recoverable only via CLI/manual SQL.

Severity high is correct: this is an availability/lockout defect on the privileged platform-admin surface (including the break-glass support console), trivially triggerable by an attacker who knows an admin email, with no in-band recovery. Not 'critical' because it is not cross-tenant data breach, money loss, or data corruption — it is denial-of-administration with an operational (CLI/SQL) recovery path.

Proposed fix is sound: on successful verify() also reset status (`status: admin.status === 'locked' ? 'active' : admin.status`), or — cleaner and matching the tenant LoginService — stop overloading status for transient lockout and gate solely on lockedUntil.
exploit:
Targeted brick (attacker, knows victim admin email, e.g. owner@libriant.com):
1. POST /admin/auth/login {email: owner@libriant.com, password: "wrong"} x5 (default MAX_FAILED_LOGINS=5). No rate limiting fronts this endpoint (the only throttler is on support-key redemption, admin-support.controller.ts:90).
2. On the 5th attempt admin-auth.service.ts:62-71 sets failedAttempts=5, lockedUntil=now+15min, AND status='locked'.
3. The 15-min lockedUntil window expires. Nothing ever flips status back to 'active' — success branch (lines 75-78) and the MFA controller (mfa.controller.ts:79-87) both leave status untouched; no admin-users mgmt controller exists.
4. The real admin now logs in with the CORRECT password: verify() passes (it does not check status==='locked'), POST /admin/auth/login returns 200 and sets a valid cookie. But EVERY guarded /admin/* request — incl GET /admin/auth/me (admin-auth.controller.ts:47) and all support/fleet/tenants routes — hits AdminAuthGuard (admin-auth.guard.ts:30) and returns 403 'Your admin account is no longer active.'
5. The console is unusable. Only recovery: run scripts/bootstrap-admin.ts (sets status:'active', bootstrap-admin.ts:66 — but also force-resets password) or manual SQL `UPDATE admin_users SET status='active' WHERE email=...`.

Self-inflicted variant: an admin who fat-fingers their password 5 times bricks their own account identically. title: TOTP codes are replayable — MFA verify has no used-step tracking, gating cross-tenant impersonation
description: verifyToken does `return verifySync({ token, secret, epochTolerance: 30 }).valid` (mfa.service.ts:88) — no `afterTimeStep` and no persisted last-step. otplib 13.4.0 supports replay protection: types-BBT_82HF.d.ts:116-119 'Rejects tokens with timeStep <= afterTimeStep', and the impl defaults `afterTimeStep:t.afterTimeStep` to undefined (functional.js). With period 30, epochTolerance:30 accepts ±1 step (~60-90s live window). A grep for mfaLastStep/lastStep/afterTimeStep/totpStep across apps/api/src and the control schema returns nothing — no replay state exists. verifyToken gates the redeem flow at admin-support.controller.ts:103, which mints the impersonation cookie (lines 132-137).
impact: An observed valid admin TOTP code can be replayed within ~90s. Combined with a captured support key this yields a cross-tenant impersonation session. Partial mitigation: the redeem rate limit (5/min/admin, 10/min/IP at admin-support.controller.ts:254-284) caps volume, but a single replay still succeeds and one redeem is enough. TOTP single-use guarantee is defeated for the most sensitive action in the system.
fix: Persist the last-accepted time step per admin (a column or short-TTL Redis key) and pass otplib 13's `afterTimeStep` to reject steps <= last accepted; also tighten epochTolerance to asymmetric [30,0] (past-only) to halve the window.
skepticReasoning:
Premise verified against the real otplib 13.4.0 source, not just the type stubs.

1) No replay state, code-confirmed:
- apps/api/src/support/mfa.service.ts:88 calls `verifySync({ token, secret, epochTolerance: 30 }).valid` — it passes NO `afterTimeStep` and discards the returned `.timeStep`.
- In node_modules/.pnpm/otplib@13.4.0/.../otplib/dist/functional.js, the wrapper builds `afterTimeStep:t.afterTimeStep` (undefined here) and forwards it to the TOTP `verifySync`.
- In @otplib/totp@13.4.0/dist/index.js, the sync verify loop (`ie`) skips a step only via `w(t,u){return u!==void 0 && t<=u}` — when `afterTimeStep` (`u`) is undefined this is always false, so no step is ever rejected as replayed. The result object exposes `timeStep` precisely so callers can persist it for replay protection; mfa.service.ts ignores it.
- Window math confirmed: @otplib/core normalizeEpochTolerance(30) -> [30,30]; with period 30 the verify setup `R` computes minCounter=current-1, maxCounter=current+1, i.e. a +/-1 step window. A code is accepted for its own 30s step plus the two neighbors ≈ 60–90s.
- Grep across apps/api/src and packages/db-control/prisma for afterTimeStep/lastStep/totpStep/usedStep/mfaUsed returns no replay-tracking state. AdminUser schema (schema.prisma:324-328, 730-734) has only mfaSecretCipher/mfaNonce/mfaKeyId/mfaEnabled — no last-accepted-step column. So no replay state exists anywhere.

2) This TOTP is the SOLE second factor for the most sensitive action. Admin login is password-only (apps/api/src/admin/admin-auth.controller.ts:33-37 + admin-auth.service.ts verify() — bcrypt password only, no TOTP). The only places verifyToken is called are mfa.controller.ts:75 (one-time enrollment) and admin-support.controller.ts:103 (redeem). The redeem TOTP is the only barrier between a password/cookie-compromised admin session and a 4-hour cross-tenant impersonation JWT minted at admin-support.controller.ts:132-137 via ImpersonationSessionService.sign. Defeating TOTP single-use therefore degrades the one MFA gate protecting cross-tenant impersonation. RFC 6238 mandates rejecting reused codes; that guarantee is broken.

I tried hard to refute it and found two real partial mitigations that lower it from critical to high but do not eliminate it:
- The support key is genuinely single-use: support-session.service.open() (support-session.service.ts:52-61) flips the key to status='redeemed' in the same tx, and verifyAndConsume only matches status:'pending' (support-key.service.ts:141). So a byte-for-byte replay of a *completed* legitimate redeem fails on the key, not the TOTP. The replayed TOTP must be paired with a *different* still-pending key.
- The redeem rate limit (5/min/admin, 10/min/IP — support-rate-limit.ts:16-20) caps volume but a single replay still succeeds, and one redeem is enough.

Net: a real, exploitable degradation of a security-critical second factor, but it requires the attacker to also hold an authenticated admin session plus a separate pending support key, so it is high (serious security weakness / defense-in-depth failure), not critical (no standalone one-step breach).
exploit:
Concrete exploit (phishing-relay / captured-request variant, cross-tenant):
1. Attacker compromises admin Alice's password or session cookie (phishing, credential stuffing, stolen cookie via XSS/extension, or a relay proxy). Admin login needs no TOTP (admin-auth.controller.ts:33-37), so this yields a valid /admin/* session usable against /admin/support/redeem (gated only by AdminAuthGuard, admin-support.controller.ts:63).
2. Attacker possesses or captures a still-pending support key K2 for victim tenant T2 (e.g., captured alongside a legitimate redeem in a relay/MITM, or a key handed out for an unrelated tenant the attacker controls visibility into).
3. Attacker observes ONE valid 6-digit TOTP from Alice within ~60-90s — via the relay page capturing the real redeem POST (code+totp), a keylogger, or shoulder-surf.
4. Within the ±1-step window, attacker POSTs /admin/support/redeem with Alice's cookie + key K2 + the observed TOTP. mfa.service.ts:88 returns valid (no used-step check), keys.verifyAndConsume matches pending K2, sessions.open mints a session, and admin-support.controller.ts:132-137 issues a 4-hour impersonation JWT into T2 — a cross-tenant impersonation session obtained by replaying a single observed code that, under RFC-correct single-use TOTP, would already be dead.

Reproduction of the core defect (deterministic): call mfa.verifyToken(secret, code) twice with the same valid code inside the same 30s step (or within +/-30s); both return true. With proper tracking the second call must return false. The otplib API already supports this: verifySync(...).timeStep gives the accepted step; persisting it per admin and passing afterTimeStep (plus epochTolerance:[30,0] for past-only) closes the window.

Refutation attempts that FAILED to clear it: byte-identical replay is blocked by the single-use key flip (support-session.service.ts:52-61), and rate limiting caps volume — but neither stops a single replay paired with a second pending key, and one successful redeem suffices. The defect is real.

title: Unauthenticated /auth/signup has no rate limit and forks a migration subprocess + CREATE DATABASE per request
description: POST /auth/signup has no guard/throttle (auth.controller.ts:48-58). main.ts wires only cookieParser, the HttpExceptionFilter, and shutdown hooks — no ThrottlerModule, no helmet (grep for ThrottlerModule/@nestjs/throttler/helmet across apps/api/src and package.json returns nothing). signup → provision → createDatabase runs raw `CREATE DATABASE "${dbName}" ENCODING 'UTF8'` (tenant-provisioning.service.ts:126) and applyTenantMigrations shells out via execFileP('pnpm', ['exec','prisma','migrate','deploy'], ...) per signup (tenant-provisioning.service.ts:150).
impact: A script POSTing unique slugs can mass-provision tenants, each creating a real Postgres database and forking a Prisma migration subprocess — exhausting Postgres DB/connection limits, disk, and CPU/memory, and littering every cell with junk DBs requiring manual teardown. Low-effort DoS against platform operations.
fix: Put strict rate limiting + bot protection (Turnstile/CAPTCHA) in front of /auth/signup, queue provisioning instead of running it inline, cap concurrent provisioning, and add per-IP and global signup quotas.
skepticReasoning:
Confirmed after attempting refutation. POST /auth/signup is unauthenticated and unthrottled: auth.controller.ts:48-58 has only validateDto + @HttpCode, no @UseGuards/@Throttle/captcha (contrast complete-setup at line 79 which carries @UseGuards(AuthGuard)). main.ts wires only cookieParser + HttpExceptionFilter + shutdown hooks — no ThrottlerModule, no helmet, no global rate-limit guard. app.module.ts's only global provider is SupportAuditInterceptor; the global middleware chain (Session/Admin/Impersonation/SystemMode/Tenant) does not throttle, and SystemMode does not block /auth/* in normal modes. The codebase's sole rate limiter (support-rate-limit.ts) is scoped to the admin support-redeem endpoint only.

The work per request is real and inline: signup.service.ts:85 calls provisioner.provision(...) synchronously in the request path with NO queue, NO concurrency cap, and NO per-IP counter. provision() runs CREATE DATABASE "${dbName}" (tenant-provisioning.service.ts:126), then opens the new DB and runs 4 CREATE EXTENSION statements (lines 132-141), then forks a full Node/Prisma subprocess via execFileP('pnpm',['exec','prisma','migrate','deploy']) per signup (line 150). SignupDto enforces slug shape + uniqueness, but a script trivially mints unique slugs, so the ConflictException pre-flight does not stop the attack.

Refutation attempts and why they fail: (1) Caddy edge — infra/caddy/Caddyfile reverse-proxies /lbr-api/* but contains NO rate_limit directive; its own comment (lines 141-145) says it forwards CF-Connecting-IP 'so audit logs + rate limits key off it', yet nothing downstream consumes it. (2) Cloudflare in front (Caddyfile:91-101) gives baseline DDoS protection but there is no configured CF rate-limit rule or Turnstile challenge on /auth/signup in-repo; the line 112 comment shows CF's managed challenge only fires on the bypass path, not normal app POST traffic, so a moderate-rate, single-IP, or distributed script is not auto-blocked. Mitigation is partial and unverifiable from code; it does not eliminate the path.

Minor evidence corrections to the original finding: provisioning file is apps/api/src/provisioning/tenant-provisioning.service.ts (not under tenant/); CREATE DATABASE is line 126 and migrate-deploy fork is line 150 as claimed.

Unauthenticated repro, no session required:

  for i in $(seq 1 500); do
    s="junk-$(date +%s)-$i-$RANDOM"
    curl -s -X POST https://libriant.com/lbr-api/auth/signup \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d "{\"libraryName\":\"x\",\"slug\":\"$s\",\"fullName\":\"x\",\"email\":\"$s@example.com\",\"password\":\"aaaaaaaaaaaa\"}" &

Because provision() runs synchronously in the request handler (signup.service.ts:85) with no rate limit and no queue, a few hundred concurrent requests fork hundreds of Prisma subprocesses (CPU/memory exhaustion on the API host) and create hundreds of real Postgres databases — exhausting DB count / connection / disk limits and littering the cell with junk DBs that each require manual teardown.

title: No admin role enforcement: a "support"-role admin can hard-delete tenants, edit plans, and flip the global billing switch
description: AdminAuthGuard re-reads the row but never checks role: `select: { id: true, role: true, status: true, disabledAt: true }` then `if (!admin || admin.disabledAt || admin.status !== 'active') throw new ForbiddenException(...); return true;` (admin-auth.guard.ts:28,30-33). The schema defines two tiers — `enum AdminRole { owner // Libriant founders / leadership\n support // Libriant support staff }` (db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:54-57). Every destructive controller is gated by ONLY `@UseGuards(AdminAuthGuard)` with no role decorator: tenant HARD delete `@Post(':id/delete')` which calls `this.provisioning.teardown(tenant.id)` + `controlDb.tenant.delete(...)` (admin-tenants.controller.ts:35,148-176); plan edit `@Patch('plans/:slug')` (admin-plans.controller.ts:83,114); billing master switch `@Post()` setBillingEnabled (admin-subscriptions.controller.ts:21,32-37); global maintenance `@Post('global')` openGlobal (admin-system-mode.controller.ts:34,99-110); tenant overrides PUT/DELETE (admin-overrides.controller.ts:54,69). A grep for any role gate across apps/api/src/admin, system-mode, platform-settings returns NO authorization use of role except the session-log read filter in admin-support.controller.ts:243.

The two-tier role model provides zero actual privilege separation.

Keep read endpoints and redemption open to 'support'.

title: Admin login is password-only — no MFA gate on the admin session that authorizes tenant deletion / plan edits
description: login() takes only email+password and immediately mints the full admin cookie: `const admin = await this.authSvc.verify(dto.email.toLowerCase().trim(), dto.password); const { token, expiresAt } = this.jwt.sign({ sub: admin.id, role: admin.role }); this.cookies.setSession(res, token, expiresAt);` (admin-auth.controller.ts:37-39). admin-auth.service.verify() checks only password + lockout, never MFA (admin-auth.service.ts:60-86). MFA is consulted ONLY at support-key redemption: `if (!adminRow?.mfaEnabled) throw ...; if (!this.mfa.verifyToken(secret, dto.totp)) {...}` (admin-support.controller.ts:97-107). MFA enrollment is self-service and not required to hold an admin session (mfa.controller.ts). AdminAuthGuard never checks mfaEnabled.
impact: Phishing or credential-stuffing one admin password yields the entire admin control plane (which, per adminplane-1, can delete tenants, edit plans, flip billing, open global maintenance) with no second factor. The MFA investment protects only the narrower per-tenant impersonation, which already requires a tenant-issued key.
fix: Require a TOTP step at admin login for any admin with mfaEnabled, force enrollment before privileged use of an admin session, and/or require fresh-TOTP re-auth on the destructive owner operations the same way redemption is gated.

title: tenant-relocate --drop-source can DROP the live database after a partial/failed relocation (and even after a successful one)

title: Deploy to production is not gated on CI (typecheck/tests/migrations) passing
description: deploy.yml triggers on `on: push: branches: [main]` (lines 10-12) and the `build` job (`build:` line 45) starts straight from `steps:` with no `needs:` and no `workflow_run:` trigger referencing the `ci` workflow. ci.yml is a separate workflow (`name: ci`) on the same `push`/`pull_request` events with jobs static-checks/unit-tests/integration-tests/db-migration but no build/deploy job. The only in-repo gate in deploy.yml is the POST-deploy `Wait for health` step, which polls localhost/healthz AFTER `docker compose ... up -d --force-recreate` has already swapped in the new images. .github/ contains only workflows/ (no other config files). So a push to main that fails typecheck/lint/tests/migration still builds + ships images to GHCR and force-recreates containers fleet-wide.
impact: A red CI does not block a production deploy. Code that fails typecheck, a unit/integration test, or has a broken migration is built and force-recreated on every fleet host regardless; rollback is manual and out-of-band. MEMORY.md confirms 'pushing main deploys to prod'.

NOTE: branch protection is a server-side GitHub setting not visible in-repo, so it cannot be ruled out from the repo alone — but nothing in the workflow files themselves gates the ship.

title: No DB uniqueness on outstanding fine per loan — accrual sweep racing a return double-charges the member
description: Accrual sweep does find-then-create with NO surrounding transaction: `const existing = await client.fine.findFirst({ where: { loanId: loan.id, status: 'outstanding' }... }); if (existing) {...} else { await client.fine.create({ data: { ... status: 'outstanding' } }) }` (fine-accrual.job.ts:96-119). Return flow does the same find-then-create inside its tx: fine.findFirst at loans.service.ts:464-467, fine.create at :475-485. The ONLY fine indexes are non-unique: `CREATE INDEX "fines_memberId_status_idx"` (migration:353) and `CREATE INDEX "fines_loanId_idx"` (migration:356). No partial unique index exists across all 5 tenant migrations (grep confirmed). The two code paths take no shared lock — accrual is cron-triggered, return is HTTP-triggered — so both findFirst calls can return null and both creates succeed → two outstanding fines on one loan.
impact: A member is billed twice for the same overdue when the hourly accrual sweep and a librarian's return of that loan interleave. Real money error; no DB safety net. Window is narrow (must hit the same overdue loan concurrently) but recurs across many tenants/loans over time, and there is zero enforcement preventing it.
fix: Add a partial unique index `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX fines_one_outstanding_per_loan ON fines("loanId") WHERE status='outstanding' AND "loanId" IS NOT NULL;` and handle the resulting P2002 in both paths (re-read + update existing). Note LoansService.translate (loans.service.ts:842-854) currently has NO P2002 branch, so add one there too. Optionally take a pg_advisory_xact_lock on the loan id in the accrual per-loan work and wrap it in a transaction so it serializes with the return.
skepticReasoning:
Confirmed after reading the real code, the migrations, the Prisma schema, the cron registry, and the surrounding lock/isolation behavior. The premise holds on every point:

1. Accrual sweep does an UNTRANSACTED find-then-create. `accrueOneTenant` (apps/api/src/jobs/fine-accrual.job.ts:69-123) has NO `$transaction` (grep confirmed none in the file). Lines 96-99 `client.fine.findFirst({ where: { loanId, status: 'outstanding' }})` and lines 109-119 `client.fine.create({ ... status: 'outstanding' })` are two separate autocommit statements.

2. Return flow does the same find-then-create inside its tx (apps/api/src/loans/loans.service.ts:464-467 findFirst, :475-485 create), using `client.$transaction` (line 381) with NO explicit isolation level and NO row lock on the fine/loan (grep for Serializable/isolationLevel/advisory/FOR UPDATE returned nothing).

3. No uniqueness exists. The Fine model has only `@@index([memberId, status])` and `@@index([loanId])` (schema.prisma:447-448), and the only migration confirms non-unique `fines_memberId_status_idx` (migration.sql:353) and `fines_loanId_idx` (:356). The only fines constraints are `fines_amount_nonneg` (:497) and `fines_paid_consistency` (:544). No `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` on fines anywhere in packages/db-tenant (grep confirmed). No `fine.upsert` anywhere.

4. The two processes are genuinely concurrent: the sweep runs in the separate worker process (apps/api/src/worker.ts) on an hourly schedule (registry.ts:41-44), while return is HTTP-triggered in the API process.

Refutation attempts that FAILED to mitigate it:
- Read Committed (Postgres default, used by both) has no predicate locks, so a SELECT on (loanId, status='outstanding') does not block the other transaction's INSERT of a matching row. Both findFirst can return null, both create succeed.
- The FK-insert lock does not serialize the race: an INSERT into fines referencing the loan takes FOR KEY SHARE on the loan row, while the return's `UPDATE loans SET status='returned'` takes FOR NO KEY UPDATE — these two modes are COMPATIBLE in Postgres (status is not a key column, PK unchanged), so the FK insert neither blocks nor is blocked by the status flip.
- The accrual create does not re-check loan status before inserting, and even returned loans still satisfy the FK (loanId FK is ON DELETE SET NULL, loan row still present), so flipping status='returned' doesn't reject the insert.
- `translate` (loans.service.ts:842-854) has only a check-constraint branch and pass-through — no P2002 handling — consistent with the absence of any unique index to violate.

Strong corroborating signal: the codebase uses partial unique indexes as the standard dedup mechanism for exactly this find-then-create pattern on EVERY other comparable table — collections_slug_unique_active (collections.service.ts:116,156), reservations partial unique index (reservations.service.ts:137), announcement-delivery partial unique indexes (announcement-delivery.service.ts:225), member-number partial unique index (members.service.ts:189). The fines table is the lone exception, performing the same race-prone pattern with no DB safety net.

Severity high (not critical): the outcome is a real money error — a member double-billed for one overdue — but it requires a timing race (hourly sweep interleaving with a return of that same overdue loan within the find→create window), is not attacker-controllable, and has limited blast radius per occurrence. It is a genuine correctness/reliability defect with zero enforcement, recurring across tenants/loans over time.
exploit:
Concurrent-interleaving repro (Read Committed, the default for both code paths):

Preconditions: a tenant with overdueFinesEnabled=true, finePerDayCents>0, and an active loan L past its dueAt with NO outstanding fine yet.

Timeline:
- t0: hourly fine-accrual sweep starts; accrueOneTenant loads L via loan.findMany(status='active', dueAt<now) (job:82-85).
- t1: a librarian returns L over HTTP; LoansService.return opens its $transaction (loans.service.ts:381).
- t2: Return executes findFirst(loanId=L, status='outstanding') → null (loans.service.ts:464-467).
- t3: Accrual executes findFirst(loanId=L, status='outstanding') → null (job:96-99). Neither sees the other's row: the accrual insert hasn't happened/committed, and the return's tx hasn't committed.
- t4: Accrual fine.create(...status:'outstanding') commits row A (job:109-119).
- t5: Return's tx fine.create(...status:'outstanding') commits row B (loans.service.ts:475-485).

Result: two 'outstanding' fines on loan L. There is no unique index, no advisory lock, and no Serializable isolation to reject either insert; the FK-insert lock (FOR KEY SHARE on the loan) is compatible with the return's status UPDATE (FOR NO KEY UPDATE), so nothing serializes them. The member is billed twice for the same overdue.

Note the inverse ordering (return commits first, then accrual) is also broken: even if return's create at t5 had committed before accrual's findFirst, accrual would still find it (idempotent), but the lost-update window between the two NULL-returning findFirsts is exactly what the missing partial unique index would close.

Proposed fix is correct: add `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX fines_one_outstanding_per_loan ON fines("loanId") WHERE status='outstanding' AND "loanId" IS NOT NULL;`, handle P2002 in both create sites by re-reading and updating the existing row, and add a P2002 branch to LoansService.translate (loans.service.ts:842-854), which currently has none.

title: Restoring a lost copy never closes the lost loan, permanently blocking re-checkout (unhandled P2002)

title: ReDoS: admin-defined field regex pattern runs synchronously on the shared event loop with no safe-regex guard

title: Hold promoted by reservation-expiry sweep never sets readyAt → patron never gets 'hold ready' email
description: reservation-expiry.job.ts:134-142 promotes the next hold with `data: { status: 'ready', fulfilledByCopyId: copy.id, expiresAt: new Date(...), queuePosition: null }` — no `readyAt`. The three other promotion sites ALL set it: reservations.service.ts:497 `readyAt: now` (promoteNextHoldInTx), reservations.service.ts:216 `readyAt: now` (create-as-ready), loans.service.ts:405 `readyAt: now` (return-promotes-hold). There is no status='ready' ⇒ readyAt NOT NULL constraint (migration.sql:519-540 only couples 'queued' and 'fulfilled').

They are never emailed their book is waiting, miss the pickup window, the copy re-expires, and the queue churns. This is the sweep's primary purpose, so it hits the common path. The spec (reservation-expiry.job.spec.ts) never asserts readyAt, so the drift is uncaught.
fix: Add `readyAt: now` to the promotion update in expireOneTenant (reservation-expiry.job.ts:136-141) to match promoteNextHoldInTx. Add a spec assertion that the promoted reservation has readyAt set.

title: fine-accrual sweep can double-create an outstanding fine (no unique constraint on Fine.loanId) racing the return flow
