DTOs expose the restore flag: members.dto.ts:160 `archived?: boolean` (documented at 157 "Restore from archive (true → null archivedAt + status=active)"), books.dto.ts:182, collections.dto.ts:66.

Archiving genuinely frees a slot, closing the loop: members.service.ts:426-429 sets `{ archivedAt: new Date(), status: 'archived' }`; books.service.ts:396 archive() → update({archived:true}) → archivedAt=new Date(). Both drop the row out of its active-only counter.

No DB-level backstop exists. Searched packages/db-tenant/prisma — all CHECK constraints are on field formats/values (isbn, slug regex, amount>=0, etc.); there is NO trigger, current_count column, or count-vs-quota constraint. The only quota authority is application code, and the restore paths bypass it entirely.

Intent corroboration (refutation attempt failed): the team DOES enforce quota on an un-archive restore in field-definitions.service.ts — enforceWithinTx (128) runs BEFORE the archived-row restore at 148 (`if (existing?.archivedAt) return tx.fieldDefinition.update({ data: { archivedAt: null, ... } })`), counted by the same `{ entityKind, archivedAt: null }` counter (133). That proves enforcing-on-restore is the correct, intended pattern — and that members/books/collections deviate from it. (The skeptic note that field restore "lives in a CREATE path" is irrelevant to whether the row is counted: it restores an existing archived row that the counter would then include, exactly like the members/books/collections case.)

Severity high (not critical): the limit can be pushed to (number of archived rows) above ceiling, so blast radius is real plan-revenue circumvention / resource over-consumption, but it is data-integrity/billing-bypass within a single tenant, not cross-tenant breach or data loss.
exploit:
Tenant at its plan ceiling (e.g. max_books = N, N active books) authenticated as a library admin:

Simplest form (if any archived rows already exist): PATCH /t/:slug/books/:id with body {"archived": false} on a previously-archived book. books.service.ts:347-348 sets archivedAt=null with no enforceWithinTx → active count becomes N+1. Repeat per archived row. Same for members (PATCH /t/:slug/members/:id {"archived": false}, members.service.ts:336-339) and collections (PATCH /t/:slug/data-model/collections/:cslug {"archived": false}, collections.service.ts:176).

Self-sustaining loop to grow active count arbitrarily (bounded only by archived inventory):
1. Archive one book: DELETE /t/:slug/books/:id (books.service.ts:396 → archivedAt set) → active = N-1, frees a slot.
2. Create a new book: POST /t/:slug/books (passes create-time enforceWithinTx since used=N-1 < N) → active = N.
3. Restore the archived book: PATCH /t/:slug/books/:id {"archived": false} (no check) → active = N+1.
4. Repeat with another archived book each cycle → N+2, N+3, ...

Each cycle nets +1 active book above the billed ceiling. Identical loops work for members and custom collections. Note: impersonation deliberately bypasses quotas (quota.interceptor.ts:70) but that is admin-only and irrelevant; a normal tenant admin triggers this on standard PATCH routes. No DB constraint, trigger, guard, or middleware intercepts the over-limit restore.

Fix matches proposal: in each update() restore branch, when a row transitions archivedAt non-null→null (members also status leaving 'archived'), run quota.enforceWithinTx inside the existing/added transaction with the same counter + advisory-lock key the create path uses (books: count {archivedAt:null} key max_books; members: count {archivedAt:null, status:{not:'archived'}} key max_members; collections: count {archivedAt:null} key max_custom_collections), mirroring field-definitions.service.ts:128.

title: Per-tenant DB role isolation (TenantDbCredential) is never implemented — tenant DBs accessed as Postgres superuser
description: tenant-create.ts:151 `const dbUrl = urlForDb(reqEnv('PG_SUPERUSER_URL'), dbName);` — the tenant connection string is built straight off the superuser URL. That dbUrl is written verbatim into tenants.dbUrl (lines 178-179) and never derived from a dedicated role. Grep across packages/scripts/apps shows TenantDbCredential/roleName/encryptedPwd appear ONLY in db-control/schema.prisma:279-295, the init migration (migration.sql:92-93), and the package re-export (db-control/src/index.ts:41) — never in any provisioning script or runtime code. `CREATE ROLE`/`CREATE USER`/`createRole` match nothing in the repo. At runtime tenant-prisma.service.ts:72 `makeTenantPrismaClient({ databaseUrl: ctx.dbUrl })` connects with that superuser-derived URL (ctx.dbUrl traces to tenants.dbUrl). createTenantDatabase (tenant-create.ts:265-291) only CREATE DATABASE + extensions, no role.
impact: Every per-tenant DB is opened as the Postgres superuser `libriant`, which owns all other tenant DBs and the control DB on the same instance. The intended per-tenant-role boundary does not exist, so any SQL-injection or logic flaw in a tenant-scoped request runs with superuser rights across all tenants and the control plane. The TenantDbCredential encryption/rotation machinery (encryptedPwd/encryptionKeyId/encryptionNonce) is dead schema.
fix: After CREATE DATABASE, CREATE ROLE tenant_<id> LOGIN with a random password, REVOKE CONNECT ... FROM PUBLIC, grant the role only its own DB, store the AES-GCM-encrypted password in TenantDbCredential, and build tenant.dbUrl from that role; have TenantPrismaService decrypt+use it. If superuser-per-tenant is an accepted MVP tradeoff, delete the misleading TenantDbCredential model + comments so the posture isn't overstated. Note: for the stated 5-20-tenant single-instance pilot this is defense-in-depth, not an active breach, so high (not critical) is appropriate.
skepticReasoning:
Confirmed after attempting refutation. Per-tenant DB role isolation is genuinely never implemented; tenant DBs are accessed as the Postgres superuser.

EVIDENCE (every claim verified against source):
1. Both provisioning paths derive the tenant URL from the superuser URL, not a dedicated role.
   - CLI: scripts/tenant-create.ts:151 `const dbUrl = urlForDb(reqEnv('PG_SUPERUSER_URL'), dbName);` stored verbatim to tenants.dbUrl at lines 178-179.
   - Runtime signup path (the real prod path): apps/api/src/provisioning/tenant-provisioning.service.ts:105-109 urlForDb() only swaps u.pathname (DB name) on this.env.pgSuperuserUrl, preserving the same user+password; apps/api/src/auth/signup.service.ts:122 stores placement.dbUrl on the tenant row.
2. No role isolation anywhere. grep for CREATE ROLE / CREATE USER / GRANT / REVOKE against the DB matches nothing in scripts, runtime, or infra/compose/postgres-init.sql. createDatabase() (tenant-provisioning.service.ts:111-142) and createTenantDatabase() (tenant-create.ts:265-291) only CREATE DATABASE + extensions.
3. Runtime connects with superuser creds: apps/api/src/tenancy/tenant-prisma.service.ts:72 makeTenantPrismaClient({ databaseUrl: ctx.dbUrl }) where ctx.dbUrl traces to tenants.dbUrl.
4. In production the role IS a superuser: infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:244 POSTGRES_USER: libriant (official postgres image bootstraps this user as SUPERUSER), and lines 36+71 reuse the same libriant creds for both CONTROL_DATABASE_URL and PG_SUPERUSER_URL. postgres-init.sql creates no other role. So the API/worker open every tenant DB as the cluster superuser that owns the control DB and all sibling tenant DBs.
5. TenantDbCredential is dead schema: it appears ONLY in packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:279-295, the init migration migration.sql:92-95, and the re-export db-control/src/index.ts:41 — never written or read. encryptedPwd/encryptionKeyId/encryptionNonce are inert. Comments (env.ts:204; schema.prisma:277-278) overstate the posture.

WHY HIGH NOT CRITICAL: I checked for a live weaponization vector and found none today — tenant-scoped raw SQL uses parameterized tagged templates (quota.service.ts:63; reservations.service.ts:189/343/515; loans.service.ts:412) and $queryRawUnsafe is confined to controlDb with internal args. The harm is the absent security boundary, so this is defense-in-depth for the stated 5-20-tenant single-instance pilot, exactly matching the claimed severity.
exploit: No live exploit today (premise of the finding itself acknowledges this and rates it high, not critical). Repro of the missing boundary: provision a tenant via /auth/signup or pnpm tenant:create; inspect tenants.dbUrl in the control DB — it equals PG_SUPERUSER_URL with only the database name changed (postgresql://libriant:<POSTGRES_PASSWORD>@postgres:5432/tenant_<id>), i.e. the superuser libriant. The API/worker (tenant-prisma.service.ts:72) hold a superuser session to each tenant DB. Latent attack path: any future SQL-injection or logic flaw in a tenant-scoped request would execute with superuser rights, allowing cross-tenant reads/writes and access to libriant_control on the same instance (e.g. `\c` to a sibling tenant_* DB, dropping/altering other tenants, reading password hashes). The intended mitigation (per-tenant LOGIN role with REVOKE CONNECT FROM PUBLIC, credential in TenantDbCredential) does not exist; that model is unused dead schema.

title: Production deploys are not gated on CI (tests/typecheck/migrations) passing
description: deploy.yml:11-12 triggers on `push: branches: [main]`; the deploy job needs only `[build, plan]` (line 119) — neither references the separate ci.yml workflow. ci.yml:4-5 is its own workflow on the same `push: branches: [main]` with jobs static-checks/unit-tests/integration-tests/db-migration. There is no `workflow_run`/`needs`/required-status linkage, so a commit that fails typecheck/tests/migration-smoke still builds an image (deploy.yml:67-89) and ships it: deploy.yml:155-156 `git fetch ... ; git reset --hard ${GIT_SHA}` then 174 `docker compose ... up -d --force-recreate`. The post-deploy gate (lines 194-211) only polls `http://localhost/healthz` returning 200 from Caddy's :80 plaintext block — it does not verify API/web readiness or migration success.
impact: A red build reaches production with no human gate between merge and prod (git reset --hard to the SHA). Per project convention a push to main deploys to prod; a broken/untested control-plane migration applied during deploy can hit the live control DB before anyone sees the CI failure.
fix: Gate deploy on CI via `on: workflow_run` (conclusion == success) or merge the test jobs as prerequisite `needs`, or enforce required status checks on main. Strengthen the post-deploy poll to hit the API /readyz and web /api/healthz rather than only Caddy's static :80 /healthz.
skepticReasoning:
CONFIRMED. I read all the relevant files and tried to refute it; the premise holds and the mitigation the fix would rely on (required status checks) is actually impossible on this repo.

1) No CI->deploy linkage. deploy.yml:10-12 triggers on `push: branches: [main]`; the deploy job (deploy.yml:117-124) `needs: [build, plan]` only — no `workflow_run`, no `needs` on ci.yml jobs, no required-status. ci.yml:1-5 is a separate workflow firing on the same `push: branches: [main]`, running static-checks/unit-tests/integration-tests/db-migration in parallel and fully independently. A red ci.yml run does nothing to stop deploy.yml.

2) The obvious mitigation does not exist and cannot exist here. `gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/main/protection` returns HTTP 403: "Upgrade to GitHub Pro or make this repository public to enable this feature." So branch protection / required status checks are not configured AND are unavailable on this plan — required checks cannot be the safety net.

3) The deploy applies migrations to the LIVE control DB. deploy.yml:174 runs `docker compose ... up -d --remove-orphans --force-recreate`. compose.prod.yml:128-147 defines a one-shot `migrate` service running `scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh`; that script (prod-bootstrap.sh:19,24,27) does `set -eu`, points `CONTROL_DATABASE_URL` at `PG_SUPERUSER_URL` (the live Postgres, bypassing pgbouncer), and runs `pnpm db:migrate:deploy` (= `prisma migrate deploy` on db-control, package.json:24). api/worker gate on it via `depends_on: condition: service_completed_successfully` (compose.prod.yml:158-160,220-222).

4) Post-deploy gate is hollow. deploy.yml:194-211 polls `http://localhost/healthz`. Caddyfile:115-123 answers `/healthz` on the plaintext `http://` block with `respond "ok" 200` directly — it never reverse-proxies to api (api:3001) or web (web:3000). And deploy.yml:174 uses `up -d` WITHOUT `--wait`, so the command returns once containers are created, not once their healthchecks (compose.prod.yml:172-177/202-207) pass. So an image that crashes the API on boot (the class of bug CI typecheck/unit/integration tests catch) still deploys "green."

Refutation attempts that FAILED to kill it: (a) "compose up will fail on a bad migration, catching it" — partly true: because of `service_completed_successfully`, a migration that THROWS makes `up -d` exit non-zero and the SSH step (set -euo pipefail, deploy.yml:153) turns red. But by then the failing migration's DDL has already partially executed against the LIVE control DB and Prisma marks it failed in `_prisma_migrations`, which then blocks every subsequent deploy until a human manually resolves it — the migration hazard is real, just self-evident rather than silent. (b) A migration that is clean-but-semantically-wrong (drops/renames a column the running code reads, destructive change that passes locally) applies successfully, `migrate` exits 0, deploy proceeds, and the hollow /healthz gate never notices — fully silent. (c) Code-only red builds (typecheck/test failures that crash the app at runtime) deploy green because no --wait and /healthz doesn't touch api/web.

Net: per project convention a push to main auto-deploys to prod, and there is no automated gate between a failing CI run and a `git reset --hard <sha>` + `compose up` that runs migrations against the live control plane. Confirmed.

Not critical because it is not directly attacker-exploitable (requires a maintainer to push a broken commit) and a hard-erroring migration is at least surfaced (deploy turns red) rather than silently corrupting; but it is a genuine production reliability/migration-safety hole with blast radius across the whole control plane, so high is correct.
exploit:
Repro 1 (broken code ships green): push a commit to main that compiles-but-crashes the API at boot, or that fails ci.yml typecheck/unit/integration. ci.yml runs and turns red in parallel, but deploy.yml runs concurrently, builds the image (deploy.yml:67-89), SSHes to the host, `git reset --hard <sha>` (156), `docker compose up -d --force-recreate` (174). With no `--wait`, `up -d` returns once containers are created. The post-deploy poll (194-211) hits `http://localhost/healthz`, which Caddyfile:115-123 answers with a static 200 independent of api/web. Deploy reports success while the API container is crash-looping in prod.

Repro 2 (control-DB migration hazard, the worst case): push a migration to packages/db-control/prisma/migrations that errors against prod data (e.g. a NOT NULL add on a column with existing nulls, or a constraint that conflicts with live rows) but passed/wasn't exercised in CI. deploy.yml:174 starts the `migrate` one-shot -> prod-bootstrap.sh:27 `pnpm db:migrate:deploy` against PG_SUPERUSER_URL (live control DB). Prisma applies the migration's statements; it fails partway, leaving the live control DB partially migrated and the migration marked failed in `_prisma_migrations`. `up -d` then exits non-zero (api won't start), so the deploy step turns red — but the live control DB is now in a failed-migration state that blocks all future deploys until manually repaired (`prisma migrate resolve`), during which signup/billing/provisioning on the live control plane are degraded. A clean-but-semantically-wrong migration is even worse: it applies fully, exits 0, deploy goes green, and the damage (e.g. a dropped/renamed column the running API reads) is live with no gate having looked at the API at all.

Cannot be triggered by an unauthenticated external attacker — it requires push access to main; the trigger is a maintainer merging/pushing a red commit, which the project's push-to-main = auto-deploy convention makes routine.

title: backup.sh pg_dumpall only covers the local cluster — relocated/other-cell tenants silently omitted
description: backup.sh dumps via `docker compose -f "$COMPOSE_FILE" -p "$COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME" exec -T postgres pg_dumpall -U libriant --clean --if-exists | gzip -9 > "$dest/postgres.sql.gz"` (lines 46-48) — only databases inside that one postgres container. The control schema models multiple cells each with their own dbHostUrl (packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:198-211, comment line 203 'Base address for tenant DBs in this cell'), and tenant-relocate.ts:1-2 / --to-cell exists to move a tenant's DB to a different cell/host. The only integrity guard is `if [ "$dump_bytes" -lt 1024 ]` (line 51), which the control DB plus co-located tenants will always exceed.
impact: Backups silently omit any tenant relocated off the primary cell or provisioned onto a secondary cell. The 1KiB size check cannot detect the gap. Combined with the missing restore tooling (ops-dr-5), a relocated tenant can be unrecoverable after a disaster despite 'successful' nightly backups. Severity high is justified for the multi-cell case; note the codebase ships single-cell for the pilot (schema comment line 195-197), so the blast radius is latent until a second cell is used — but tenant-relocate.ts is built precisely to create that situation.
fix: Drive backups from the control plane: enumerate every tenant's db_url and pg_dump each database individually with a per-DB size/success assertion, and fail the run unless the count of dumped tenant DBs matches the active control-plane tenant count. Single-cluster pg_dumpall is only safe while there is provably exactly one cell.

title: No restore script exists — DR restore path is untested/undocumented beyond a comment
description: backup.sh comment at lines 44-45 claims 'pg_dumpall writes a single self-contained script — restoring is `psql -f`.' A repo-wide search confirms NO restore tooling exists: `find . -iname '*restore*'` (excluding node_modules) returns nothing, and `grep -rln 'pg_restore|restore|psql -f' scripts/ infra/deploy/` matches only scripts/tenant-relocate.ts (its pg_restore) and the backup.sh comment. scripts/ contains backup.sh but no restore.sh/restore.ts. Per-tenant DBs require extensions unaccent/pg_trgm/pgcrypto/citext created at provision time (scripts/tenant-create.ts:284-287) and re-created during relocate (scripts/tenant-relocate.ts:248-251) — none of which a bare `psql -f` of pg_dumpall output is verified to restore.
impact: The recovery half of backup/restore is paper-only. A real restore would be done ad hoc under incident pressure with no validation that the dump restores cleanly, that per-tenant extensions are present, or that storage.tar.gz files map back to the right tenant ids. High risk of botched/partial recovery and extended downtime at the worst moment.
fix: Write and periodically exercise a restore script (scripts/restore.ts/.sh) that restores postgres.sql.gz into a clean cluster, restores storage.tar.gz, re-points db_url/storage_url, busts caches, and verifies per-tenant row counts + extension presence. Add a scheduled restore-to-scratch drill so the backup is proven recoverable.

title: Relocate is not atomic: pg_dump → pg_restore is non-blocking on the source, so writes during the dump are lost even with a perfect read_only window
description: Even if ops-dr-2's cache race were fixed, the relocate uses a snapshot-and-copy model with no fencing of the source: pg_dump takes its consistent snapshot at the moment it starts (line 113-119), the restore + verify + control-plane flip happen afterward (lines 122-150), and the source DB is never set to read-only AT THE DATABASE LEVEL (only the application-level system-mode event is used). The read_only system mode 503s mutating HTTP requests but does NOT block (a) the impersonation/admin-bypass paths that the middleware explicitly lets through (apps/api/src/system-mode/system-mode.middleware.ts:110-121: admin-bypass routes and `req.impersonation` skip the read_only check entirely), nor (b) any BullMQ worker / background job that writes directly to the tenant DB without passing through the HTTP middleware. Any such write committed to the source after pg_dump's snapshot is silently dropped on cutover.
impact: Writes from admin/support sessions (impersonation), and from any background worker that mutates the tenant DB, are not fenced during a relocation and are silently lost when db_url flips to the dumped copy. The middleware's own design (admin bypass + impersonation pass-through) guarantees at least the admin-write class can slip through.
fix: Fence at the database level for the duration: e.g. `ALTER DATABASE "<db>" SET default_transaction_read_only = on` plus terminate/deny new write backends on the source before pg_dump, or use a logical-replication/online-cutover approach. At minimum, take pg_dump after confirming zero non-idle write backends on the source and keep the source read-only (DB-level) until the control-plane flip commits.

title: Login endpoint has no per-IP throttle; lockout is per-account only → credential stuffing / horizontal brute force
description: auth.controller.ts:60-62 `@Post('login')` public, no throttle guard; app.module.ts has no APP_GUARD. The only defense is per-user: login.service.ts:107 `await this.recordFailure(user.id, user.failedLogins)` and recordFailure :160-169 increments `failedLogins` and sets `lockedUntil` only when `nextCount >= this.env.maxFailedLogins`. Password spraying keeps each account at failedLogins=1, never locking. bcrypt verify runs on every real-identifier attempt (login.service.ts:105 `this.passwords.verify`) and dummyVerify on every miss (:62,67,90,95,98), so each attempt costs CPU regardless.
impact: Credential stuffing / password spraying across a tenant's whole user base runs at full speed without tripping the per-account lockout. An attacker can also repeatedly trip one account's lockout to keep a legitimate user out (lockout-as-DoS), and the per-attempt bcrypt is a CPU-amplification vector against the API.
fix: Add a per-IP and per-(tenant,IP) request throttle on /auth/login (e.g. 10/min/IP) on top of the per-account lockout, using @nestjs/throttler with Redis so it holds across replicas; consider a per-IP failed-attempt lock. Requires the trust-proxy/X-Real-IP fix (ratelimit-5) to key on the real client.

title: Password-reset request is an unthrottled email-bomb; minute-bucket idempotency only dedups within one minute
description: auth.controller.ts:130-136 `@Post('password-reset/request')` public, no throttle. password-reset.service.ts:60 `const minuteBucket = Math.floor(Date.now() / 60_000)` and :79 `idempotencyKey: \`auth.password_reset:${user.id}:${minuteBucket}\`` — the key changes every 60s, so the email enqueue (:75-87) fires once per minute per (user) indefinitely; across minute boundaries each request enqueues a fresh email. No per-IP, per-email, or per-tenant cap exists anywhere on this path. The DTO (password-reset.dto.ts) accepts any slug+email shape, so an attacker who knows a slug+victim email can drive it.
impact: Mailbomb a known (slug,email) victim ~1 email/minute (more when straddling minute boundaries), and at scale flood the BullMQ email queue + SMTP provider, delaying legitimate mail (real resets, due-date reminders) and burning the tenant's sender reputation/quota.
fix: Rate-limit /auth/password-reset/request per IP and per (tenant,email) over a rolling window (e.g. 3/email/hour, N/IP/hour) with a Redis counter independent of the minute-bucket idempotency key; keep the uniform OK response.

title: trust proxy never set + Caddy sends X-Real-IP (not X-Forwarded-For) → req.ip is always the proxy IP, breaking the support per-IP limiter and any future IP throttle
description: main.ts:16-43 never calls `app.set('trust proxy', …)` (grep for trust/proxy over apps/api/src returns nothing). Caddyfile:146 `header_up X-Real-IP {http.request.header.CF-Connecting-IP}` inside `handle_path /lbr-api/*` and NO `header_up X-Forwarded-For` anywhere. Express derives `req.ip` from X-Forwarded-For only when trust proxy is enabled, and never from X-Real-IP — so with trust proxy off, `req.ip` is the Caddy container socket peer for every request. That `req.ip` is consumed by the only IP limiter: admin-support.controller.ts:90 `enforceRedeemRateLimit(admin.sub, req.ip)` whose IP count keys on `ipAddress: ip` (admin-support.controller.ts:262-265) against REDEEM_LIMITS.ipPerMinute=10 (support-rate-limit.ts:18), and by audit/notify rows at admin-support.controller.ts:115,127,154,298.
impact: The per-IP limb of the support-key limiter collapses to a single global counter (one shared Caddy IP), so a distributed attack evades it while a burst from any source can spuriously trip the shared IP bucket. Forensic audit rows (redeemedFromIp/ipAddress) record the proxy IP, not the attacker. Most importantly, ANY rate limiter added for ratelimit-1/2/3 will silently key on the proxy IP and protect nothing until this is fixed.
fix: Set `app.set('trust proxy', <trusted hops/subnet>)` AND read the IP from `x-real-ip` (what Caddy actually sets) via a custom key extractor, after confirming the host firewall (Caddyfile:143-145 claims Cloudflare-only ingress) truly prevents header spoofing from non-Cloudflare origins.

title: HTML attribute injection in auto-linked URLs (href breakout) via book title / member name / admin template
description:
smtp-driver.ts:69 `const escaped = md.replace(/&/g, '&').replace(//g, '>');` — the double-quote is never escaped. smtp-driver.ts:70 `const linked = escaped.replace(/(https?:\/\/[^\s<]+)/g, '$1');` — the URL class `[^\s<]+` includes `"`, and the captured text is placed inside a double-quoted href. Reproduced live with node: input `Book: http://evil.com/"onmouseover="alert(1) is due` rendered exactly as `

Book: http://evil.com/"onmouseover="alert(1) is due

` — the href is terminated early and an onmouseover attribute is injected onto the . Attacker-controlled inputs confirmed: member.fullName is free text capped only by @Length(1,200) (members.dto.ts:31-33) and book.title is free text capped only by @Length(1,500) (books.dto.ts:32-33); both quote chars pass validation. They are interpolated into bodyMarkdown in member-notifications.job.ts (dueSoon body lines 49-52, overdue 71-74, holdReady 95-96; vars built at 204-209, 240-245, 277) and the admin custom template body is substituted verbatim (substitute() at member-notifications.job.ts:103-104, pickTemplate 112-115). bodyMarkdown is stored verbatim by EmailService.enqueue (email.service.ts:106) and rendered to the html part with no intervening sanitization (email-worker.ts:128 `row.bodyMarkdown + BRAND_EMAIL_FOOTER` → smtp-driver.ts:48 `html: markdownToBasicHtml(input.bodyMarkdown)`). Only the SMTP driver renders HTML; the console driver logs plain text (console-driver.ts:18-20).
impact: Any actor who can set a book title or member full name (every librarian/admin via the normal catalog/members create-update API, plus the bulk import path under apps/api/src/import) can plant a quote-bearing URL that, when a due-soon/overdue/hold-ready reminder fires, injects arbitrary attributes onto a link in the recipient patron's HTML email. Reliable impact is stored link/UI spoofing and a mismatch between the visible URL text and the real href (phishing inside a trusted library email); escalates toward behavior/script injection in email clients that honor injected inline attributes/handlers. Affects every recipient of the affected reminder. Honest severity is high, not critical: modern email clients sanitize inline event handlers, so guaranteed JS execution is not assured, but the spoofing/attribute-injection is reliable and stored.
fix: Escape the double-quote (and single-quote) in the initial escape pass at smtp-driver.ts:69 — add `.replace(/"/g, '"').replace(/'/g, ''')` — so a URL can never break out of the href attribute. Better: build the href from a separately-escaped/validated URL (reject or truncate any match containing a quote) distinct from the displayed link text, or adopt a vetted HTML sanitizer for the email html part instead of hand-rolled regex escaping.

title: renderHtml does not sanitize; marked passes raw HTML/script through — latent stored XSS in the authenticated tenant shell
description:
scripts/ingest-help-articles.ts:92-95 `function renderHtml(markdown: string): string { marked.setOptions({ gfm: true, breaks: false }); return marked.parse(markdown, { async: false }) as string; }` — no sanitize step. title: Deploy SSH uses unpinned ssh-keyscan (trust-on-first-use) every run — MITM of root-equivalent deploy session
description: .github/workflows/deploy.yml:134-137: `- name: Add host to known_hosts` / `run: |` / `mkdir -p ~/.ssh` / `ssh-keyscan -H "${{ matrix.host.ssh }}" >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts`. The grep over .github/ scripts/ infra/ docs/ for `stricthostkeychecking|known_hosts|ssh-keyscan|fingerprint` returns only this line (plus an unrelated github.com keyscan in docs:252) — no StrictHostKeyChecking, no committed host key, no fingerprint secret anywhere. fleet.yml confirms `ssh: 178.104.32.176` is a raw public IP over the internet. The deploy session then runs `git reset --hard`, `bash scripts/ensure-env.sh --auto /srv/libriant/.env.prod`, and `set -a; . /srv/libriant/.env.prod; set +a` (deploy.yml:156,161,162), sourcing all prod secrets.
impact: An attacker able to MITM the GitHub-runner→host SSH path (BGP/route hijack, DNS/IP spoof, compromised transit) can present their own host key, have ssh-keyscan blindly trust it, and intercept the deploy session — which sources /srv/libriant/.env.prod (SESSION/ADMIN/IMPERSONATION secrets, MFA_MASTER_KEY, STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET, POSTGRES_PASSWORD) and runs arbitrary remote commands as the deploy user. Effective full prod compromise + secret exfiltration. Each runner starts with a fresh ~/.ssh so there is zero persistence/pinning — it is pure TOFU every run.
fix: Pin the host key: store the real SSH host public key as a GitHub secret and write it to ~/.ssh/known_hosts directly, then run ssh with `-o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes` (or `=accept-new` is NOT enough). At minimum capture the fingerprint once and fail the deploy if a later keyscan diverges (TOFU-with-pinning).

title: Automated ensure-env.sh --auto silently regenerates POSTGRES_PASSWORD after boot-disk loss, locking the app out of the surviving database
description: scripts/ensure-env.sh:61 `ensure_rand() { ... [ -n "$(getv "${k}")" ] || { setv "${k}" "$(openssl rand -hex "${b}")"; ... }; }` and :70 `ensure_rand POSTGRES_PASSWORD 24`: a fresh password is minted whenever the key is empty in .env.prod, with NO check of whether the DB data dir already exists. deploy.yml:161 runs `bash scripts/ensure-env.sh --auto /srv/libriant/.env.prod` unconditionally on every push to main. docker-compose.volume.yml binds `pg_data` to `${LIBRIANT_DATA_ROOT:-/mnt/libriant}/postgres` (survives Hetzner Rebuild); docker-compose.prod.yml:241 uses `postgres:16-alpine` with `POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?...}` (line 245) — the official image only applies POSTGRES_PASSWORD at initdb (empty data dir), and connection strings at lines 36/71/272 use `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}` from .env.prod. docs/deployment-hetzner.md Part 16 confirms .env.prod lives on the boot disk (wiped on Rebuild) while postgres data lives on the volume (kept), and that the operator must manually restore .env.prod ('Keep a copy of .env.prod in your password manager; it's the one thing not on the volume').
impact: On the documented OS-rebuild recovery path, if a CI deploy (push to main) reaches a freshly-rebuilt host before the operator manually restores .env.prod, --auto mints a NEW POSTGRES_PASSWORD. Postgres boots against the surviving data dir keeping the OLD password, so api/worker/migrate authenticate with the new one and fail — the app is locked out of the surviving control-plane DB (all tenant routing/billing data) until the original password is recalled. Note the deploy's `Wait for health` step (deploy.yml:183-211) would fail the deploy, so this is detected, but the lockout/availability incident on the exact 'loss-free' recovery path is real. Severity held at high; blast radius is narrowed to the rebuild-race window, which is why it is not critical.
fix: In the --auto path, refuse to mint a new POSTGRES_PASSWORD when PGDATA already exists: fail loudly if ${LIBRIANT_DATA_ROOT}/postgres is non-empty but POSTGRES_PASSWORD is unset. Alternatively persist POSTGRES_PASSWORD (or all of .env.prod) on the data volume alongside the DB it unlocks and source it from there in deploy.yml.

title: startCheckout does not enforce plan.isPublic — an owner/admin can subscribe to hidden/legacy/experimental Stripe plans by slug
description: startCheckout guards only `if (!plan || !plan.isActive || plan.archivedAt)` (billing.service.ts:217) — no isPublic check. By contrast selectPlan rejects non-public: `if (!plan || !plan.isActive || !plan.isPublic || plan.archivedAt)` (line 182), and listAvailablePlans filters `where: { archivedAt: null, isActive: true, isPublic: true }` (line 86). The slug is fully client-supplied: StartCheckoutDto.planSlug is validated only as a slug format (billing.dto.ts:5-9). The endpoint requires owner/admin (`@Roles('owner','admin')`, billing.controller.ts:45-50). schema.prisma:392 documents isPublic=false as 'Hide from public plan list entirely (legacy / experimental plans)'. So an authenticated owner/admin who knows/guesses a private plan's slug can POST /t/:slug/billing/checkout and start real Stripe Checkout against that plan's stripePriceId, bypassing the visibility gate selectPlan/listAvailablePlans enforce.
impact: A tenant can self-serve onto a deliberately-hidden plan (legacy/grandfathered price, experimental discount, partner deal) and lock in its Stripe price + feature set — a pricing/visibility-integrity bypass that is a direct money loss if private plans are cheaper or more generous than public ones. Requires the owner/admin role and knowledge of the slug, which bounds blast radius below a pure unauthenticated exploit, but it is a genuine inconsistency between the three plan-selection paths.
fix: Mirror selectPlan: in startCheckout reject non-public plans unless it's the tenant's current plan, e.g. add `|| (!plan.isPublic && plan.id !== sub.planId)` to the guard at line 217. Keep listAvailablePlans/selectPlan as the single allow-list and have checkout reuse it rather than re-deriving the gate.
skepticReasoning:
The core claim is TRUE and verified against the real code. startCheckout (apps/api/src/billing/billing.service.ts:217) guards only `if (!plan || !plan.isActive || plan.archivedAt)` with NO isPublic check, while the other two plan-selection paths both enforce visibility: selectPlan rejects `!plan.isPublic` (line 182) and listAvailablePlans filters `where: { archivedAt: null, isActive: true, isPublic: true }` (line 86). planSlug is fully client-supplied and only format-validated (billing.dto.ts:5-9). The endpoint is reachable by any tenant owner/admin (@Roles('owner','admin'), billing.controller.ts:45-50). The bypass is durable, not transient: on Checkout completion syncStripeSubscription resolves the plan by stripePriceId (line 438), writes planId onto the subscription (line 459), stamps planSelectedAt (478-481), and invalidates EffectivePlanService — so the tenant genuinely ends up on the hidden plan's price and (more generous) feature values. The Stripe driver performs no re-validation (stripe-driver.ts:85 just takes a priceId). schema.prisma:391 documents isPublic=false as exactly the legacy/experimental case.

I tried hard to refute it and found two genuine bounds that lower severity from the claimed 'high' to 'medium', but NOT to false:
1. Not exploitable against shipped seed data. The only seeded private plan, on-prem-enterprise (seed-data.ts:181-191), has billingMode='manual' and stripePriceId=null, so checkout is rejected earlier at lines 220-224 (billingMode !== 'stripe') and 225-229 (!stripePriceId). So out of the box there is no reachable target.
2. No plan-creation endpoint exists — admin-plans.controller.ts only exposes @Patch/@Put on existing plans (no @Post create). An exploitable target therefore only exists once an operator flips an existing billingMode=stripe plan that has a stripePriceId to isPublic=false via PATCH (line 126) — i.e. the documented grandfathered/legacy/replaced-pricing scenario. That is a realistic operational state, just not the default.

Net: the inconsistency is real and the bypass works end-to-end whenever such a hidden stripe-priced plan exists; it is gated behind the owner/admin role plus knowledge of an unlisted slug (slugs are not enumerable via any read endpoint since listAvailablePlans filters them out). Real money/feature-integrity impact under a realistic-but-non-default config, role-gated, no out-of-box target => medium, not high. The proposed fix (mirror selectPlan: add `|| (!plan.isPublic && plan.id !== sub.planId)` to the line 217 guard) is correct.
exploit:
Preconditions: (a) attacker holds owner or admin role in any tenant; (b) operator has a plan with billingMode=stripe, a valid stripePriceId, isActive=true, archivedAt=null, isPublic=false (e.g. a once-public 'pro' plan PATCHed to isPublic:false via /admin/plans/:slug after being replaced by a pricier successor — admin-plans.controller.ts:126); (c) attacker knows that plan's slug. Note: the shipped seed has NO such plan (on-prem-enterprise is manual/no-price), so this is not exploitable on a fresh install.

Repro: POST /t/<slug>/billing/checkout with body {"planSlug":"<hidden-stripe-plan-slug>"}. In startCheckout the guard at billing.service.ts:217 (!plan || !plan.isActive || plan.archivedAt) passes (plan is active and unarchived), billingMode==='stripe' passes (220), stripePriceId present passes (225), and plan.id !== sub.planId passes (230). Service calls stripe.createCheckoutSession with the hidden plan's stripePriceId (254). Attacker completes Stripe Checkout at the returned URL. Webhook customer.subscription.created -> syncStripeSubscription looks up the plan by that stripePriceId (438) and persists planId onto the subscription (459) + stamps planSelectedAt (478). Tenant is now durably on the hidden plan: its (cheaper) Stripe price is locked in and its (more generous) feature values apply after effectivePlan.invalidate. By contrast POST /billing/select with the same slug is rejected at line 182, and the plan never appears in GET /billing/plans (line 86) — proving the three paths are inconsistent and checkout is the hole.

Refutation attempts that FAILED to clear it: no isPublic check anywhere in the checkout path; Stripe driver does not re-validate price visibility (stripe-driver.ts); webhook keys off stripePriceId not visibility, so the change sticks; planSelectedAt stamping confirms the choice rather than reverting it. Fix: add `|| (!plan.isPublic && plan.id !== sub.planId)` to the line 217 guard, mirroring selectPlan while still allowing a tenant already on a now-private plan to re-checkout.

title: Worker /readyz never checks live Redis — reports ready while jobs silently stop draining
description: worker.ts:76 const ready = !shuttingDown && !!emailWorker && !!scheduledJobs && !!importWorker; only checks boot-time handle assignment, never connection liveness. Comment at 73-75 claims ready means 'connected to Redis' but nothing pings. Every worker opens Redis with maxRetriesPerRequest: null (email-worker.ts:61, export-worker.ts:24, scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:36, import-worker.ts:236), so ioredis retries forever on disconnect instead of erroring — handles stay non-null after a drop. Worse, the Compose restart-gating probe is /healthz (compose:233), which is even weaker: worker.ts:54 returns 200 whenever !shuttingDown regardless of Redis.
impact: A worker that lost its Redis connection keeps returning 200 on /readyz and /healthz and passing the Compose healthcheck, so the orchestrator never restarts it while the email outbox, imports, exports and all cron jobs quietly stop draining.
fix: Make /readyz ping each worker's Redis (expose connection.status === 'ready' or do a timed connection.ping()) and return 503 when any is not ready; point the Compose worker healthcheck at /readyz; add per-connection 'error'/'close' loggers and a worker-down alert.
skepticReasoning:
The code-level claims are all verified, but the finding's central MECHANISM ("the orchestrator never restarts it") is wrong, which is why I downgrade from high to medium.

VERIFIED TRUE:
- apps/api/src/worker.ts:76 — `const ready = !shuttingDown && !!emailWorker && !!scheduledJobs && !!importWorker;` only checks boot-time handle assignment, never connection liveness. (It also silently omits maintenanceWorker and exportWorker from the gate entirely.)
- worker.ts:53-54 — /healthz returns 200 whenever `!shuttingDown`, fully Redis-independent.
- All five worker Redis sockets use `maxRetriesPerRequest: null` (email-worker.ts:61, export-worker.ts:23, scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:35, import-worker.ts:236), so ioredis retries forever on a drop instead of erroring — the Worker handles stay non-null and the process never exits.
- No `error`/`close` handlers on any worker connection (only job-level `failed`/`completed`); the unused RedisService.ping() (redis.service.ts:44) is never called by the worker.
- docker-compose.prod.yml:233 — worker healthcheck is `wget http://localhost:3002/healthz`, the weaker probe.

WHERE THE FINDING IS WRONG (refutation that forces the downgrade):
1. There is NO orchestrator that restarts on healthcheck failure. Deployment is plain Docker Compose on a single Hetzner host (infra/deploy/fleet.yml) — no Swarm `deploy:`, no k8s, no autoheal/watchtower. The restart policy is `restart: unless-stopped` (compose:74), which restarts a container only on PROCESS EXIT, never on `unhealthy`. So /healthz returning 200 is NOT what blocks a restart — a 503 wouldn't trigger one either. The finding's impact ("the orchestrator never restarts it") and its proposed fix ("point the Compose worker healthcheck at /readyz") both assume a restart-on-unhealthy behavior that does not exist here.
2. A transient Redis blip self-heals: `maxRetriesPerRequest: null` makes BullMQ workers resume draining when Redis returns, so /readyz=200 during a blip is actually correct.

WHY IT STILL STANDS (medium): The genuine, unmitigated harm is the silent-failure + zero-signal gap, not a defeated restart loop. On a PERMANENT Redis topology change (container replaced with a new IP, evicted/OOM, or a wedged blocking connection), the worker never errors and never exits, so /healthz + /readyz both stay 200, Prometheus `up{job="libriant-worker"}` stays 1 (the /metrics HTTP server in worker.ts:51 is Redis-independent), and NO alert fires — alerts.yml has only `TargetDown`/`LibriantApiDown` (need the HTTP server itself down) and host/PG rules; there is no BullMQ backlog/queue-depth or worker-stall metric (worker exports only uptime + in-flight gauges, worker.ts:93-106). The email outbox, imports, exports and all cron jobs quietly stop draining with zero operator signal. Blast radius is limited to background jobs (member due/overdue/hold-ready reminder emails, import/export, Stripe webhook retry sweep, session/reservation expiry sweeps) — degraded notifications/automation, not request-path data loss or cross-tenant breach — hence medium, not high. Correct fix: have /readyz ping each worker connection (connection.status==='ready' or timed ping) AND add a Prometheus alert on worker job-stall / queue backlog plus per-connection error/close logging — since Compose won't auto-restart, the operator-facing alert is the load-bearing remediation, not the healthcheck endpoint swap the finding proposes.
exploit: Repro: bring up the prod stack (docker-compose.prod.yml), let the worker reach ready (/readyz=200). Simulate a permanent Redis loss the worker can't transparently recover from — e.g. `docker compose rm -sf redis` then recreate it so the worker's existing blocking BRPOPLPUSH connection is stale, or point Redis at a flushed/replaced instance. Result: the worker process stays alive (maxRetriesPerRequest: null → infinite retry, no throw, no exit), so `restart: unless-stopped` never fires; `curl localhost:3002/healthz` → 200 and `curl localhost:3002/readyz` → 200 (handles still non-null); Prometheus `up{job=\"libriant-worker\"}` stays 1 (metrics server is Redis-independent) so TargetDown does not fire and there is no backlog/stall alert. Meanwhile enqueue an email/import/export job or wait for a cron tick — nothing drains. Net: silent, unalerted background-job stoppage. Counter-evidence to the finding's framing: pointing the healthcheck at /readyz (its proposed fix) would NOT cause a restart on this single-host Compose deploy, because Compose never restarts on `unhealthy`; only a process exit or an external alert-driven action would. A transient (recoverable) blip self-heals and would not exhibit the stall.

title: Worker Compose healthcheck probes /healthz which never reflects Redis or queue health — a dead-but-alive worker is never restarted
description: The Docker healthcheck that gates worker restarts probes /healthz (docker-compose.prod.yml:233 'wget -qO- http://localhost:3002/healthz'). /healthz (worker.ts:53-71) returns statusCode 200 whenever !shuttingDown, regardless of whether any BullMQ Redis connection is alive or any sub-worker booted — the queues field reports 'starting' vs 'running' but the HTTP status is always 200 unless shutting down. The deeper /readyz probe (which at least checks 3 of 5 handles) is NOT used by the Compose worker healthcheck; only the web/api services probe /readyz. Combined with maxRetriesPerRequest: null on every worker connection (email-worker.ts:61 etc.), a worker whose Redis dropped, or one that never finished booting any sub-worker, stays 'healthy' to Compose forever and is never restarted.
impact: Background processing (emails, imports, exports, all cron sweeps: reservation-expiry, support-session expiry, Stripe retry) can be fully stalled while the worker container shows healthy and is never restarted. This is the restart-gating consequence of reliability-2 and uses the actual probe Compose relies on, so it is the operationally decisive variant.
fix: Point the worker's Compose healthcheck at /readyz, and make /readyz actually verify each BullMQ Redis connection status and include all required sub-workers.
skepticReasoning:
The core mechanism is real and verified against the actual code.

1. The worker's Compose healthcheck probes /healthz, not /readyz: infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:233 `test: ['CMD','wget','-qO-','http://localhost:3002/healthz']`. (Finding's path 'docker-compose.prod.yml:233' is missing the `infra/compose/` prefix, but the line number and content are exact.)

2. The worker's /healthz returns 200 whenever not shutting down, with zero awareness of Redis or sub-worker boot state: worker.ts:53-54 `if (req.url === '/healthz') { res.statusCode = shuttingDown ? 503 : 200;`. The `queues` field only reports 'running' vs 'starting' (handle non-null), and the HTTP status is unconditionally 200 unless shuttingDown.

3. The deeper /readyz (worker.ts:72-83) is NOT used by Compose, and even it is weak: it only checks `!!emailWorker && !!scheduledJobs && !!importWorker` (3 of 5 handles, no actual Redis ping).

4. The asymmetry vs api is real: the api's Compose healthcheck uses /readyz (docker-compose.prod.yml:173), and the api /readyz actively pings Redis + DB and throws 503 on failure (health.controller.ts:36-44). So the api self-heals a Redis fault via restart; the worker does not.

5. All 5 BullMQ worker connections use `maxRetriesPerRequest: null` (email-worker.ts:61, scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:35, import-worker.ts:236, maintenance-worker.ts:30, export-worker.ts:23) with NO `.on('error')` handler and NO process.exit on connection failure (grep confirmed: process.exit only at worker.ts:206 graceful-shutdown and main.ts:50 api). With `maxRetriesPerRequest: null`, BullMQ's blocking commands queue forever on a persistent Redis fault instead of erroring — the worker idles, the HTTP server stays up, /healthz stays 200, and Compose never restarts it.

6. The single worker runs every cron in the registry (jobs/registry.ts): support-session-expiry, reservation-pickup-expiry, stripe-webhook-retry, fine-accrual, export-file-cleanup, announcement-publish, book-metadata-refresh, member-notifications — plus the email outbox drain. All stall together.

7. No compensating alert exists: infra/monitoring/alerts.yml has only TargetDown (`up == 0` — won't fire because the worker's HTTP/metrics server stays alive during a Redis stall) and LibriantApiDown (scoped to job=libriant-api only). There is no worker-down, queue-depth, or stalled-jobs alert, and the monitoring stack is a separate optional overlay that may not be deployed.

I tried to refute it and partially succeeded on severity, not existence: the 5 BullMQ sockets rely on ioredis's DEFAULT retryStrategy (unlike the shared RedisService at redis.service.ts:22-31 which sets explicit retry + enableOfflineQueue:false + maxRetriesPerRequest:3), so a brief Redis blip will usually auto-reconnect and self-heal. The failure only becomes permanent under a *sustained* Redis fault (OOM/credential rotation/network partition/corruption) or a boot-time outage. It also causes processing delay, not hard data loss (emails sit in a retryable EmailOutbox; most crons are idempotent and resume on next restart). That is why I downgrade from the claimed 'high' to 'medium': the decisive premise is correct, but it requires a triggering fault and the blast radius is delayed-processing, not data/money loss or cross-tenant breach.
exploit:
Repro (sustained Redis fault): deploy the prod stack; let the worker boot healthy. Then make Redis persistently unavailable to the worker — e.g. `docker kill libriant-redis` and keep it down, or simulate an OOM/partition lasting beyond ioredis reconnect. The worker's 5 BullMQ connections (maxRetriesPerRequest:null, no error handler) stop draining queues: no emails sent, no reservation-pickup-expiry, no stripe-webhook-retry, no fine-accrual, no member-notifications. The Node HTTP server in worker.ts is independent of BullMQ, so `wget http://localhost:3002/healthz` still returns 200 (worker.ts:54), the Compose healthcheck (docker-compose.prod.yml:233) stays passing, and the container is never restarted. Prometheus `up` stays 1 (so TargetDown never fires) and there is no worker-down/queue-depth alert, so nobody is paged. Contrast: the api container hitting the same Redis fault flips /readyz to 503 (health.controller.ts:43) and gets restarted by its /readyz-gated healthcheck (docker-compose.prod.yml:173).

Boot-time variant: start the worker with Redis unreachable. email/import/maintenance handles are set synchronously (no Redis await — see email-worker.ts:94 returning immediately after `new Worker`), so they're non-null; scheduledJobs awaits `queue.getRepeatableJobs()`/`queue.add()` (scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:43,57) which hang under maxRetriesPerRequest:null, so its handle never gets set. Either way /healthz returns 200, Compose marks the worker healthy, and no restart is attempted to retry the boot — all background processing is dead while the container shows healthy.

Fix matches the proposed one: point the worker Compose healthcheck at /readyz (docker-compose.prod.yml:233) and make worker /readyz (worker.ts:72) actually verify each BullMQ connection's status (and ideally check all 5 sub-workers, not 3), so a dead-but-alive worker fails the probe and gets restarted.

title: Hard-deleting a tenant leaves stale resolver cache + open Prisma client pointing at the dropped DB
description: Confirmed the controller only injects two services — admin-tenants.controller.ts:39-42: `constructor(@Inject(TenantProvisioningService) private readonly provisioning, @Inject(EffectivePlanService) private readonly effectivePlan)`. The delete handler does teardown (line 168 `await this.provisioning.teardown(tenant.id)`), purgeStorage (172), `controlDb.tenant.delete` (176), and only `this.effectivePlan.invalidate(tenant.id)` (178). No call to TenantResolverService.invalidate() or TenantPrismaService.forget(). admin.module.ts:27-48 does NOT import TenantModule, so neither service is even injectable here. TenantResolverService caches the full context under `tenant:slug:<slug>` for ttlSec (env.ts:162 default 300). TenantPrismaService LRU holds the live client (tenant-prisma.service.ts:37-54, updateAgeOnGet:true, ttlAutopurge:false).
impact: For up to TENANT_CACHE_TTL_SEC (300s) after a hard-delete, requests to /t/<slug>/... still resolve from the Redis cache as status:'active'; TenantGuard passes for anyone holding a valid session cookie; getClient() returns the cached open PrismaClient pointing at a DROPped database, so queries 5xx. On shutdown the LRU dispose/onModuleDestroy also tries to $disconnect a client whose DB is gone (caught, harmless). NOTE: the finder's cross-tenant / DB-name-reuse scenario does NOT apply — tenant.id is @default(cuid()) (db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:219), so a deleted tenant's cuid (and thus its deterministic dbNameFor `tenant_<id>`) is never regenerated; there is no path to silently reconnect to a freshly-recreated DB of the same name. The real consequence is a bounded ~5-minute window of 5xx errors on a deleted slug, not data loss or cross-tenant breach — hence medium, not high.
fix: Have AdminModule import TenantModule, inject TenantResolverService + TenantPrismaService, and in the delete handler call tenantPrisma.forget(tenant.id) BEFORE teardown() and resolver.invalidate({ slug: tenant.slug, customSubdomain: tenant.customSubdomain }) after the control-row delete. Fetch customSubdomain in the lookup select (currently only id/slug/name/storageUrl at line 158).

title: Suspending or archiving a tenant has no cache-invalidation path — paused libraries stay reachable for up to the cache TTL
description: Confirmed the middleware gates purely on the cached status — tenant.middleware.ts:76 `if (ctx.status === 'archived') throw new GoneException(...)` and 79 `if (ctx.status === 'suspended') throw new ForbiddenException(...)`, where ctx comes from the resolver cache (tenant-resolver.service.ts:73 returns the cached tenant; status is in tenantSelect at line 122). Repo-wide grep for writes of tenant status to 'suspended'/'archived' returns ZERO hits across apps/ and scripts/ (only reads like tenant-migrate.ts:68 `where.status = { not: 'archived' }`). resolver.invalidate() callers are only auth.controller.ts:55 and admin-tenant-tags.controller.ts:72. So there is no in-app path that flips status AND busts the cache.
impact: If an operator suspends/archives a tenant by raw SQL (the only mechanism that exists today), the resolver cache keeps serving status:'active' for up to TENANT_CACHE_TTL_SEC (300s), so the 403/410 gate never fires and the library stays fully reachable during that window — a real but operationally narrow access-control gap. Downgraded from high to medium: there is no in-app suspend/archive feature to regress (the bug is latent until such a feature ships or until raw-SQL suspension is used), and an operator doing the SQL edit can mirror the relocate script's redis-del to bust the cache. It becomes high the moment an in-app suspend button is added without invalidation.
fix: Add a dedicated admin status-change endpoint that, in the same handler, updates tenant.status and calls resolver.invalidate({ slug, customSubdomain }) (and tenantPrisma.forget on archive). Until then, document that suspend/archive SQL must be followed by deleting Redis keys lbr:tenant:slug:<slug> / lbr:tenant:sub:<sub>, or cache status separately under a much shorter TTL.

title: No IP/global rate limiting on login or password-reset; reset has only a per-user minute bucket
description: Tenant login defends only with a per-account lockout keyed on user.id in recordFailure (login.service.ts:160-177); no IP/global throttle exists anywhere (no ThrottlerModule in the app). password-reset request uses only `idempotencyKey: \`auth.password_reset:${user.id}:${minuteBucket}\`` (password-reset.service.ts:79 with minuteBucket at line 60), which suppresses duplicate emails within one 60s window for the SAME user but does not cap distinct requests or distinct targets.
impact: Credential stuffing / password spraying across many accounts (one attempt each, never tripping a single account's counter) is unthrottled at the IP/global layer. The reset endpoint can email-bomb arbitrary registered users (one per minute per target, unbounded targets) and churn Redis token entries / SMTP quota. Per-account lockout does not cover spray attacks.
fix: Add Redis-backed IP-scoped and global rate limiting (e.g. @nestjs/throttler) on /auth/login, /auth/signup, /auth/password-reset/request and /complete; for reset also throttle per source IP and per target email.

title: Tenant sessions are never revalidated against the DB — deactivated/suspended/password-reset users keep working sessions for the full 7-day JWT TTL
description: Tenant AuthGuard only checks that req.session exists (auth.guard.ts:13), and SessionMiddleware sets req.session purely from JWT signature+expiry (session.middleware.ts:25-26). TenantGuard adds only a tid==tenant.id comparison from the JWT, no DB lookup (tenant.guard.ts:46-54). Neither path ever re-reads the user row, so user.status, role changes, lockout, or a password reset/change have no effect on an already-issued JWT until it naturally expires (sessionTtlSec default 7*24*60*60 = 7 days, env.ts:166). This is explicitly asymmetric with the admin side: AdminAuthGuard re-reads the DB every request precisely so 'a disabled admin's existing session is invalidated immediately, not at next sign-in' (admin-auth.guard.ts:13-32). password-reset.complete() and login.completeSetup() rotate the passwordHash but cannot invalidate live JWTs (no token version / no DB check).
impact: A tenant user who is deactivated (status set to disabled/suspended), role-downgraded, or whose account is recovered via password reset retains a fully functional session — including all tenant data access — for up to 7 days. An attacker holding a stolen/active session survives the victim's password reset, defeating the primary account-recovery remediation. Offboarding a librarian/volunteer does not take effect until their JWT expires.
fix: Have AuthGuard/TenantGuard re-read the user row per request (mirroring AdminAuthGuard) and reject non-active users, OR add a session/token version column bumped on password change/deactivation and verified on each request; shorten the tenant JWT TTL and rely on sliding refresh.

title: Stale parallel support sessions: redeeming for a second tenant orphans the first as 'active' for its full 4h TTL
description: open() ends prior sessions ONLY for the same tenant: `await tx.supportSession.updateMany({ where: { tenantId: input.tenantId, endedAt: null }, data: { endedAt: new Date(), endedReason: 'admin_ended' } });` (support-session.service.ts:35-38). The impersonation cookie has a single fixed name (env.ts:191-194), so redeeming tenant B overwrites the cookie that pointed at tenant A (admin-support.controller.ts:137). endMySession ends only the most recent active session: `findFirst({ where: { adminId: admin.sub, endedAt: null }, orderBy: { startedAt: 'desc' }, select: { id: true } })` then ends just that one (admin-support.controller.ts:212-218). Tenant A's row stays endedAt=null until its TTL; LibrarySupportController.activeSession (library-support.controller.ts:76-105) will keep showing it as live to tenant A.
impact: Tenant A's library sees an 'active' support session (with the admin's name + expiry) for up to the 4h TTL after the admin moved to tenant B, and the admin's 'End session' button won't close A. Misrepresents who currently has access in a trust-sensitive UI; cleanup relies on TTL expiry or the library manually revoking.
fix: On open(), also end any other active session belonging to the same admin (where adminId = input.adminId, endedAt null), or forbid a second concurrent redemption while one is open; alternatively end the session the replaced impersonation cookie pointed at.

title: No trust-proxy configuration: per-IP redemption rate limit and recorded redeemedFromIp reflect the load balancer, not the admin
description: main.ts never calls app.set('trust proxy', ...) (grep for trust proxy in apps/api/src returns nothing). Production topology is `Internet → Cloudflare → Caddy → api` (infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:5,85-110 — Caddy is the only ingress) and Caddy reverse_proxies to api:3001 (infra/caddy/Caddyfile:139-146,180-182). With Express trust proxy OFF, req.ip is the socket peer = Caddy's container IP. The redeem limiter keys the per-IP limit on req.ip: `controlDb.supportRedemptionAttempt.count({ where: { ipAddress: ip, ts: { gte: oneMinuteAgo } } })` (admin-support.controller.ts:262-265, ip from req.ip at :90), and audit/notification paths record req.ip (admin-support.controller.ts:115,127,154,298). Notably the real client IP IS available — Caddy sets `header_up X-Real-IP {http.request.header.CF-Connecting-IP}` (Caddyfile:146,182) — but the code reads req.ip, not that header.
impact: The 10/min/IP throttle collapses into a single global counter for all traffic behind Caddy (one admin can throttle everyone; a distributed attacker is folded to one IP), and redeemedFromIp / attempt ipAddress / the library notification email all record Caddy's internal IP instead of the real client — undermining forensic attribution. The per-admin (5/min) and failed-per-hour (10/hr) limits still function since they key on adminId.
fix: Set Express trust proxy for the deployment (e.g. app.set('trust proxy', 1) after confirming Caddy/Cloudflare sanitize X-Forwarded-For) or read the already-populated X-Real-IP/CF-Connecting-IP header for the IP-based limit and audit columns.

title: Webhook event can be permanently lost if the process hard-crashes between Redis SETNX and dispatch completion (dedup lock outlives a never-processed event the sweep won't rescue)
description: Order is: SETNX with 30-day TTL (stripe-webhook.controller.ts:71-77), best-effort upsert of the DB row with processedAt=null/error=null (lines 83-95, errors swallowed), then dispatch (line 98). The Redis lock is only released via `redis.client.del` inside the dispatch CATCH block (line 116) — i.e. only on a thrown error, not on a hard crash (SIGKILL/OOM) during dispatch. On a hard crash after SETNX succeeds, Stripe never got 2xx and retries, but the retry hits the still-present key, SETNX returns non-OK, and the handler returns `{received:true, deduped:true}` (lines 78-80) doing no work. The retry sweep only picks rows with `error: { not: null }, processedAt: null` (stripe-retry.job.ts:37), so the crash-left row (error=null) — or no row at all, if the crash beat the upsert — is never replayed. The DB upsert is NOT authoritative for dedup (Redis is), confirming the gap.
impact: A hard crash in this window silently drops one billing event for the 30-day dedup TTL with no automatic recovery. Depending on the lost event (subscription.deleted, payment_failed, plan change) a tenant is left over- or under-entitled. The timing window requires a hard crash (not a thrown error, which is handled), so it's narrow, but the failure is silent and unbounded by the system's own retries.
fix: Persist the DB row BEFORE taking the Redis lock so a row always exists, and broaden the sweep to also pick up `processedAt IS NULL` rows older than a few minutes regardless of error; or treat the DB row's processedAt as the authoritative dedup check with Redis as a fast-path only, so a lock with no processed row re-runs.

title: Branding logo downloads are broken — 'branding' is missing from the storage controller's RESOURCE_TYPES allow-list
description: storage-demo.controller.ts:26 `const RESOURCE_TYPES: readonly ResourceType[] = ['covers', 'members', 'attachments', 'marc'];` — omits 'branding'. The ResourceType union DOES include it (storage-driver.ts:20 `export type ResourceType = 'covers' | 'members' | 'attachments' | 'marc' | 'branding';`) and ALLOWED_TYPES includes it (allowed-types.ts:17 `branding: ['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/webp'],`). branding.controller.ts:62-79 stores refs like `branding/<id>.png` on `brandLogoRef`. The ONLY ref-serving route is GET `t/:slug/storage/:resourceType/:filename` (storage-demo.controller.ts:80) which calls parseResourceType (line 88), and parseResourceType throws BadRequestException for anything not in RESOURCE_TYPES (lines 165-169). The web shell builds the logo URL `/lbr-api/t/${params.slug}/storage/${session.tenant.brandLogoRef}` (layout.tsx:159-160) and the settings preview `/lbr-api/t/${slug}/storage/${logoRef}` (BrandingForm.tsx:31); next.config.mjs:23 proxies `/lbr-api/:path*` straight to the API, so resourceType resolves to 'branding' → HTTP 400. Confirmed no other route serves `branding/` refs (grep: only the branding controller's upload/delete handlers reference the prefix).
impact: The per-library header logo feature (commit d01f7f7) is non-functional: upload succeeds and brandLogoRef persists, but every that points at the logo gets HTTP 400 / broken image, in both the tenant shell header and the branding settings preview. Storage is silently consumed by logos that can never render.
fix: Add 'branding' to RESOURCE_TYPES on storage-demo.controller.ts:26 so it matches the ResourceType union and ALLOWED_TYPES. The render call sites (shell header, settings preview) are all behind a valid tenant session, so TenantGuard will pass once the allow-list accepts the type; no separate public route is needed for these two uses. Add an end-to-end test that GETs a branding/ ref.

title: Whole file and fully-materialized row array held in memory (no streaming) under a 64 MB upload cap
description: import-worker.ts:100 `const data = await readStaged(batch.stagingPath)` (import-staging.ts:30-32 `fs.readFile` → whole file Buffer), :101 `parseByFormat(...)` with NO maxRows → csv-parser.ts:127 `decodeBuffer` (whole string) + :132 `tokenize` (full string[][] matrix) + tabular.ts:62-78 materializes every row as a `{rowNumber, cells}` object into `rows[]`; xlsx-parser.ts:42 `wb.xlsx.load(ab)` loads the whole workbook + :54-61 builds the full matrix. runner.ts:50 `const total = table.rows.length` + :53 `for (const raw of table.rows)` iterates the fully-materialized array. Upload cap is 64 MB (import.constants.ts:7) and import worker concurrency is 1 (import-worker.ts:253). worker.ts:123-173 boots email, scheduled, import, maintenance AND export workers in one process.
impact: A large legitimate migration file (or a crafted many-column file maximizing per-cell object overhead) can OOM the worker; because all five queues share one process (worker.ts:123-173), an import OOM also kills email delivery, scheduled sweeps, maintenance and exports platform-wide. No row-count ceiling exists on the commit path (only the preview uses maxRows: PREVIEW_ROWS, import.service.ts:48-54/18).
fix: Stream rows via a streaming CSV reader and exceljs WorkbookReader, pulling rows through an async iterator in executeImport. Short term: add a row-count ceiling (reject files whose row count exceeds N) and/or lower IMPORT_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES, and isolate the import worker in its own process so an OOM doesn't take down email/scheduled jobs.

title: No cold-start recovery for imports stuck in validating/committing (contradicts code comment)
description: import-worker.ts:11-12 comment claims processImportJob is exported so it can be driven from 'a cold-start recovery sweep'; grep confirms processImportJob is only called from the BullMQ Worker (import-worker.ts:246) and tests — no sweep. jobs/registry.ts (lines 1-9) has no import entry; worker.ts boots no import recovery scan. BullMQ retries disabled: import-queue.service.ts:35 `attempts: 1`. On restart mid-commit the batch stays 'committing'; requireRunnable (import.service.ts:322-324) only allows uploaded/validated, assertEditable (import.service.ts:309-314) blocks remap, and remove() (import.service.ts:227-229) refuses to delete a committing batch. Only cancel() (import.service.ts:215-223, no status guard) escapes — slightly less 'permanent' than the finder states, but partial rows remain committed and the staging file leaks until a manual cancel+delete.
impact: A worker restart (deploy/OOM/crash) during commit strands the batch in 'committing' with partially-written tenant rows and a leaked staging file; no automatic recovery re-drives or fails it. User must manually cancel then delete; nothing tracks where the partial commit stopped.
fix: Implement the promised startup recovery sweep: find batches in validating/committing with no active BullMQ job and re-enqueue or mark failed; persist a processed-row cursor so a resumed commit can skip already-written rows; and allow remove()/staging cleanup for a stale running batch after a timeout.

title: CSV/XLSX formula injection: member- and book-supplied text written to cells with no =/+/-/@ neutralization
description: toCsv esc() at line 274: `return /[",\n\r]/.test(s) ? \`"${s.replace(/"/g, '""')}\`` : s;` — only quotes cells containing " , CR or LF; never prefixes a leading = + - @ \t. cellValue() line 262: `if (typeof v === 'number' || typeof v === 'boolean' || typeof v === 'string') return v;` — strings pass through verbatim. Exported tables include free text writable by tenant staff: Member.fullName/addressLine1/addressLine2/staffNotes/customFields (schema.prisma:315-336) and Book.title/description (schema.prisma:212-229). MembersController (members.controller.ts:42-44) and BooksController (books.controller.ts:33-34) are guarded by TenantGuard ONLY — no @Roles — so any signed-in tenant user (incl. non-admin staff) can plant the payload. A grep of apps/api/src found zero formula-neutralization helpers in the export path.
impact: Stored-then-exported formula injection. A lower-privileged tenant staff account plants `=HYPERLINK/WEBSERVICE/DDE` text in fullName/staffNotes/title etc.; when a higher-trust owner/admin opens the CSV/XLSX in Excel/Sheets the formula executes in their context. The most serious angle is the admin 'all' scope export (export-processors.ts:179-188), which aggregates EVERY active tenant's tables into one bundle the platform operator opens — a malicious tenant staffer's payload crosses into the platform operator's desktop. Severity reduced from high to medium vs. the original because the writer must be an authenticated tenant user, not an anonymous patron, but the cross-tenant-to-operator path keeps it a genuine production risk.
fix: Add formula neutralization for string cells in BOTH toCsv esc() and cellValue(): if the string's first char is one of = + - @ \t \r, prefix a single quote (') before writing. Apply to strings only; keep numbers/dates/booleans typed. Standard OWASP CSV-injection mitigation.

title: Relocate/storage-migrate leave the tenant in a read_only (503-for-writes) window on failure with no auto-expiry
description: openReadOnly() (tenant-relocate.ts:197-211, storage-migrate.ts:169-181) creates a SystemModeEvent with `mode: 'read_only'` and NO `endsAt` (schema endsAt is nullable, default unset — schema.prisma:956). The window is closed only by closeEvent() on the success path (tenant-relocate.ts:157, storage-migrate.ts:129). The catch (tenant-relocate.ts:160-163, storage-migrate.ts:132-135) rethrows without closing: 'read_only window stays open for inspection.' SystemModeService.activeWhere (system-mode.service.ts:199-211) treats the row as active while `endedAt IS NULL AND (endsAt IS NULL OR endsAt > now)`, and the middleware (system-mode.middleware.ts:123-128) returns 503 for POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE under read_only. There is no scheduler/auto-close (service comment 29-35: 'we never run a scheduler'); only manual endNow() (service.ts:126-136) ends it. The dangling event id is logged only on open (line 106 / 90).
impact: A transient failure during pg_dump/restore/verify or rsync strands the tenant in read-only: writes 503 indefinitely until an operator manually finds and ends the event. Reads still work (GET passes), and this is an operator-run CLI, not an automatic path, so blast radius is one tenant and recovery is one SQL update — hence medium, not high.
fix: Set an `endsAt` (e.g. now+30m) on the read_only event so an aborted run self-heals, or close the window in a finally block once the tenant is confirmed still on the source. At minimum, on the failure path print the exact endNow/SQL command with the event id.

title: Provisioning + maintenance run `prisma migrate deploy` with the Postgres superuser URL passed via child-process env
description: applyTenantMigrations() builds targetUrl from pgSuperuserUrl (provision() line 61 → urlForDb 105-109 swaps only the path on `this.env.pgSuperuserUrl`) and execs with `env: { ...process.env, TENANT_DATABASE_URL: targetUrl }` (line 152). Same pattern in maintenance-processors.ts:289-293 (migrateDeploy) and 426-430 (migrateStatus), and the scripts (tenant-migrate.ts:126-130). env.ts:203-208 documents PG_SUPERUSER_URL as 'the libriant superuser' in dev / 'a dedicated provisioning role per cell' in prod. Every per-request tenant self-migration at signup and every fleet maintenance migrate therefore runs the tenant DDL through a CREATE-DATABASE-capable credential materialised in a child process env (readable via /proc/<pid>/environ).
impact: Day-to-day app/migration path runs with cluster-superuser rights rather than a per-tenant owner role. A malicious/compromised migration file, leaked process env, or migration-supply-chain issue executes with rights to read/alter every tenant DB and CREATE/DROP DATABASE — widening blast radius from one tenant to the whole cell. Severity medium: requires PROD to actually point PG_SUPERUSER_URL at a true superuser (the env comment says it may be a scoped provisioning role).
fix: Provision each tenant DB with a dedicated owner role scoped to that DB and run migrate deploy as that role; reserve the superuser strictly for CREATE DATABASE / extension install. Pass credentials via a transient file or stdin rather than inherited env, and document that PG_SUPERUSER_URL must be a least-privilege provisioning role in prod.

title: Reservation-expiry cron flips a copy to reserved with an unguarded update (no status check) — can clobber an on_loan copy
description: Cron: `const copy = await tx.bookCopy.findFirst({ where: { bookId: r.bookId, status: 'available' } })` (line 125-127, plain SELECT, no FOR UPDATE) then `await tx.bookCopy.update({ where: { id: copy.id }, data: { status: 'reserved' } })` (lines 143-146) — unconditional, no `status: 'available'` guard. No isolationLevel and no advisory lock anywhere in this job (grep: only placeHold at reservations.service.ts:189 uses pg_advisory_xact_lock), so it runs at Read Committed. The safe equivalents guard: promoteNextHoldInTx uses `updateMany({ where: { id, status: 'available' }, ... })` and checks flipped.count (reservations.service.ts:503-507), and checkout uses `updateMany({ where: { id, status: expectedCopyStatus } })` + count check (loans.service.ts:289-297).
impact: If a librarian checks out that exact available copy (committing on_loan + creating a loan) in the window between the cron's findFirst and its update, the cron's unconditional UPDATE overwrites on_loan with reserved, detaching the copy from its now-active loan — copy shows reserved while a live (returnedAt=NULL) loan exists. Narrow window; silently corrupts rather than failing loudly.
fix: Use `tx.bookCopy.updateMany({ where: { id: copy.id, status: 'available' }, data: { status: 'reserved' } })` and skip/abort the promotion when count===0, mirroring the service path.

title: Reservation-expiry cron frees the held copy with an unguarded update — clobbers a manually lost/damaged copy back to available
description: When expiring a ready hold the cron frees its copy with `await tx.bookCopy.updateMany({ where: { id: r.fulfilledByCopyId }, data: { status: 'available' } })` (lines 108-113) — keyed on id ONLY, with NO `status: 'reserved'` guard. The equivalent service path (ReservationsService.resolveReservation) deliberately guards: `tx.bookCopy.updateMany({ where: { id: existing.fulfilledByCopyId, status: 'reserved' }, data: { status: 'available' } })` (reservations.service.ts:335-338) precisely to avoid overwriting a librarian's manual action.
impact: If staff manually marked the held copy lost/damaged/withdrawn after it was reserved-for-pickup but before the pickup window lapsed, the expiry sweep silently flips it back to 'available', un-doing the staff action and putting a lost/damaged copy back into circulation. Silent state corruption, same class as holds-race-1 but on the copy-free side.
fix: Add the `status: 'reserved'` guard to the updateMany at reservation-expiry.job.ts:109-112, mirroring reservations.service.ts:335-338.

title: TOCTOU race in member archive: active-loan/hold check is not atomic with the archive write
description: members.service.ts:411-416 `const [activeLoans, activeReservations] = await Promise.all([client.loan.count(...), client.reservation.count(...)])` then 426-429 `const updated = await client.member.update({ where: { id }, data: { archivedAt: new Date(), status: 'archived' } })` — no $transaction, no row lock, no re-check inside the write. Confirmed the counterpart path doesn't compensate: loans.service.ts:157-171 reads member status/archivedAt OUTSIDE its transaction, and the checkout $transaction at loans.service.ts:224 re-validates only the reservation and copy, never re-checking member.status/archivedAt. So a checkout (or hold) interleaving between the count and the update leaves an archived member with active circulation.
impact: An archived member can end up holding an active loan/queued hold, violating the method's stated guarantee and confusing reminders, the get() circulation summary, and restore flows. Blast radius limited to concurrent archive-vs-checkout timing on the same member.
fix: Run the count checks and the status update in one `client.$transaction`, and either take `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the member row in both archive() and the loan/hold create transactions, or re-validate member status inside the loan checkout tx (loans.service.ts:224). A DB trigger blocking new loans when status='archived' would make it order-independent.

title: Archiving a book COPY bypasses the on_loan transition guard — an on-loan copy can be soft-deleted while its loan stays active
description: CopiesService.archive() calls update({ archived: true }) (copies.service.ts:171-173). In update(), the status-transition guard only runs when an explicit status is supplied: `if (input.status && input.status !== existing.status) { ... ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS ... }` (copies.service.ts:122-133). Archive passes NO status, so the guard is skipped entirely and the write at copies.service.ts:159-161 just sets `data.archivedAt = new Date()`, leaving `status` as 'on_loan'. ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS['on_loan'] = [] (line 46) is meant to make on_loan copies untouchable except via Loans, but archive sidesteps it. The copies controller exposes this directly: DELETE /t/:slug/catalog/copies/:copyId → archive() (copies.controller.ts:45-47).
