impact: A copy that is physically checked out (status='on_loan') can be archived, removing it from default copy lists (archivedAt=null filter) while its Loan row stays status='active'. This is a stronger, more concrete version of catalog-1: the loan now points at a soft-deleted copy, return/overdue/reporting flows show an active loan against a hidden copy, and the copy's on_loan status can never be cleared through the normal Copies UI. Medium because it produces a durable inconsistent state on a normal (non-concurrent) single request, not just a race.
fix: In CopiesService.update/archive, refuse to set archivedAt when existing.status === 'on_loan' (mirror the ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS intent), e.g. throw the same 'currently checked out — return it through Loans first' error. Apply the same check before book archive in books.service.ts for copies that are on_loan.

title: reservation-expiry sweep claims a copy without the compare-and-swap guard the service uses → copy can be double-allocated
description: reservation-expiry.job.ts:125-127 `const copy = await tx.bookCopy.findFirst({ where: { bookId: r.bookId, status: 'available' } })` then 143-146 `await tx.bookCopy.update({ where: { id: copy.id }, data: { status: 'reserved' } })` — an unconditional write-by-id that does NOT re-assert status='available'. The canonical path guards the identical write: reservations.service.ts:503-511 `const flipped = await tx.bookCopy.updateMany({ where: { id: candidateCopyId, status: 'available' }, data: { status: 'reserved' } }); if (flipped.count === 0) throw ConflictException(...)`. The return flow uses the same CAS guard (loans.service.ts:451-458). The sweep's $transaction (line 100) sets no isolationLevel, so it runs at Prisma's default READ COMMITTED; the plain update-by-id will overwrite a copy a concurrent checkout already committed to 'on_loan', whereas the CAS would have caught it (count===0).
impact: If a concurrent checkout/hold-fulfill claims the exact copy the sweep just picked, the sweep blindly resets it to 'reserved', double-committing one physical copy to two members. Real data-integrity hazard but downgraded from high to medium: it requires concurrency on the same physical copy within the 60s sweep window AND the sweep typically re-grabs the copy it just freed (fulfilledByCopyId, already 'reserved'-bound to the expired hold) rather than contending with walk-in checkouts. Blast radius is one copy, recoverable at the desk.
fix: Replace the plain `update` at reservation-expiry.job.ts:143-146 with `updateMany({ where: { id: copy.id, status: 'available' }, data: { status: 'reserved' } })` and roll back / skip the promotion when count===0, mirroring promoteNextHoldInTx (reservations.service.ts:503-511).

title: Readiness probe ignores maintenance + export workers — silent queue stall reported as healthy
description: worker.ts:76 `const ready = !shuttingDown && !!emailWorker && !!scheduledJobs && !!importWorker;` — maintenanceWorker and exportWorker (declared lines 48-49, started lines 158-173) are excluded. Each is started with `.catch((err) => { console.error(...) })` (lines 162-164, 171-173) that only logs, leaving the handle null on a boot failure. With both null, /readyz still returns 200.
impact: If startMaintenanceWorker() or startExportWorker() rejects at boot (Redis hiccup, bad config), /readyz keeps returning 200 and the orchestrator leaves the pod in rotation while the maintenance and export queues accumulate jobs with no consumer. Operator migrate/vacuum/fix runs and admin-requested DB exports queue forever and never produce output, with nothing flipping readiness or alerting. /healthz does surface queues.maintenance/export as 'starting' (worker.ts:64-65) so it is not totally invisible, but readiness — the signal the orchestrator acts on — is wrong. Medium: degraded background functionality, no data loss.
fix: Include maintenanceWorker and exportWorker in the readiness predicate at worker.ts:76 (or treat a persistently-null handle as degraded), so a failed boot of either pulls the pod out of rotation.

title: Scheduled-job health snapshot only records successes — a continuously failing cron looks healthy
description: scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:82-94 writes `lastResults[job.name]` only inside the try after a successful `def.handler(ctx)` (lines 84-87); the catch is absent and only the `finally { inFlight-- }` runs. worker.on('failed') at lines 98-100 only `console.error`s — it never writes lastResults. /healthz surfaces `scheduledLastResults: scheduledJobs?.lastResults()` (worker.ts:67). The repeatable job is added with no `attempts`/`backoff` (lines 56-67: only repeat.every, removeOnComplete/Fail), so a failing tick is retried only at the next interval.
impact: If fine-accrual, stripe-webhook-retry, member-notifications, etc. start throwing every tick (bad tenant DB URL, Stripe outage), /healthz keeps showing the last SUCCESSFUL run's timestamp+message, so monitoring scraping /healthz never detects the outage — fines silently stop accruing, webhooks stop being replayed, hold-ready emails stop. Note each sweep already has internal per-tenant error isolation (e.g. fine-accrual.job.ts:51-54, reservation-expiry.job.ts:58-61) so a single-tenant failure won't throw the whole handler; the gap bites when the handler ITSELF throws (controlDb down, Redis for sub-services down). Medium ops blind spot.
fix: Record failures into lastResults (with an error flag + timestamp) from worker.on('failed') or a catch in the handler at scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:82-94, and/or emit a failure metric. Optionally add small attempts/backoff to the repeatable job.

title: Fine-accrual sweep's amount UPDATE is not transactional and can revert a return-flow finalisation (lost write)
description: When an outstanding fine already exists, the sweep updates it with the *running accrual* amount: fine-accrual.job.ts:100-107 `await client.fine.update({ where: { id: existing.id }, data: { amountCents: amount, reason } })`, using `client` directly (no transaction, READ COMMITTED, no version/status guard). The return flow finalises the SAME fine in its return transaction: loans.service.ts:468-473 updates `amountCents`/`reason` for the still-'outstanding' fine. If the hourly sweep reads the fine as outstanding, computes its accrual amount, and writes it AFTER the return transaction committed the final (possibly capped/grace-adjusted) amount but the loan-status read by the sweep was stale, the sweep can overwrite the return flow's finalised amount with its own recomputed value. The sweep keys overdue loans on `status: 'active'` (fine-accrual.job.ts:83) so a loan returned mid-tick should normally be skipped — but the loan list is read once at line 82 before the per-loan loop, so a return that commits between that read and the per-loan fine.update can still be clobbered. Blast radius: the fine amount, not duplication.
impact: A just-finalised overdue fine can be silently reset to the sweep's running-accrual figure, diverging from what the return flow recorded (e.g. ignoring a return-time waiver/cap adjustment). Member is billed the wrong amount. Lower likelihood than queue-3 (requires the loan to still read 'active' in the sweep's batch) but same root cause: no transactional coupling between sweep and return on the shared Fine row.
fix: Re-read loan status inside the per-loan step (or guard the fine.update with `where: { id, status: 'outstanding', loan: { status: 'active' } }` via updateMany) so a fine whose loan was returned mid-tick is not overwritten; ideally run the sweep's per-loan find/update in a Serializable transaction.

title: Storage quota is a lock-free check-then-write with a best-effort, droppable counter
description: put() reads the cached counter and compares with no advisory lock: storage.service.ts:68 `const currentBytes = await this.currentUsedBytes(tenant.id);` (currentUsedBytes is a plain findUnique, lines 174-180), line 70 `if (currentBytes + newSize > limitBytes) throw 402`, then writes the driver at line 87 `const stored = await driver.put(input);`. The counter bump is explicitly best-effort and swallowed: lines 92-101 `await controlDb.tenant.update({ ... storageUsedBytes: { increment: stored.sizeBytes } }).catch((err) => this.logger.warn(...))`. Unlike books/members/collections, there is no pg_advisory_xact_lock around read→write, so N concurrent uploads all read the same currentBytes and all pass (overshoot up to N×fileSize), and a dropped increment leaves the file on disk while storageUsedBytes is permanently undercounted.
impact: Concurrent uploads can exceed max_storage_mb by a bounded amount; more importantly a dropped counter bump silently and persistently under-counts storage so subsequent quota checks under-report usage and let the tenant keep uploading past their real limit. Blast radius is worse than the original brief implies because the claimed reconciliation is NOT automatic (see new finding storage-recompute-never-scheduled) — drift only heals when a human manually hits the admin recompute endpoint. Medium is correct: it is a real intermittent quota-enforcement weakness for a billed resource, but bounded and not directly exploitable into unbounded free storage. Confidence ~0.85.
fix: Serialize the check + counter mutation under a control-plane advisory lock keyed on (tenantId,'max_storage_mb'), and make the increment atomic with the success path rather than fire-and-forget. On a failed increment, either roll back driver.put or schedule an immediate targeted recompute for that tenant instead of only logging.

title: Storage usage reconciliation (recomputeUsage) is never scheduled — counter drift heals only via a manual admin endpoint
description: storage.service.ts:30-32 documents recomputeUsage as 'run nightly in prod', and put()'s best-effort counter comment (lines 89-91) claims 'the nightly recompute job (and recomputeUsage below) reconciles' a dropped storageUsedBytes increment. But there is NO such job. The only caller of recomputeUsage is the admin/demo controller route POST /t/:slug/storage-admin/recompute (storage-demo.controller.ts:135-139). The scheduled-jobs registry (registry.ts:22-71) contains support-session-expiry, reservation-pickup-expiry, stripe-webhook-retry, fine-accrual, export-file-cleanup, announcement-publish, book-metadata-refresh, member-notifications — and explicitly notes '60 min — nightly-ish stats jobs (none today)' and '24 h — heavy batch (none today)'. So any storageUsedBytes drift (from the dropped .catch in put() lines 97-101 or the dropped .catch in delete() lines 153-157, or from put-succeeds-then-process-crashes-before-increment) is PERMANENT until a human manually triggers the admin recompute endpoint per tenant.
impact: The self-healing premise that downgrades quota-3 from a hard quota hole to a transient one does not actually exist. A tenant whose increment was dropped under-reports storage forever and can keep uploading past max_storage_mb; conversely a dropped decrement permanently over-reports and can wrongly 402 a paying tenant out of storage they freed. Both are silent until someone notices and runs the manual recompute. This is a billed-resource accuracy bug independent of the race in quota-3.
fix: Register a scheduled job (e.g. daily) that walks tenants and calls StorageService.recomputeUsage, matching the code comments. Alternatively make the put/delete counter mutation atomic with the file operation (transactional outbox or compensating action on failure) so drift cannot accumulate, and remove the misleading 'nightly recompute job' comments if no such job is intended.

title: BullMQ Redis runs with allkeys-lru eviction — queued jobs/emails can be silently evicted
description: Line 289: command: ['redis-server', '--appendonly', 'yes', '--maxmemory-policy', 'allkeys-lru']. Line 37 shares the same instance with the app cache via REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379. Every BullMQ worker connects to env.redisUrl (email-worker.ts:60, export-worker.ts:22, scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:34, import-worker.ts:235). BullMQ's documented requirement is maxmemory-policy noeviction; allkeys-lru would evict BullMQ's own job/wait/active/repeat keys under pressure. NOTE: no explicit --maxmemory is set, so eviction never actually fires until a memory cap is reached.
impact: If a maxmemory cap is ever set (or a Docker mem limit is added), live BullMQ job state (queued reminder/password-reset/announcement emails, scheduled cron keys) can be evicted silently with no error or retry. With no cap today, Redis instead grows until the host OOM-kills it (AOF+restart recovers). Real latent data-loss footgun and the wrong policy for queue keys; downgraded high->medium because eviction is not currently armed.
fix: Run a dedicated BullMQ Redis (or separate DB/instance) with --maxmemory-policy noeviction; keep allkeys-lru only for the pure cache. Set an explicit maxmemory with headroom and add a Redis-memory alert.

title: No stop_grace_period and untimed pg_dump can block worker shutdown until SIGKILL
description: export-processors.ts:192-196 await execFileP('pg_dump', ['--no-owner','--no-privileges','--format=plain','--file',outPath,dbUrl], { maxBuffer: 16*1024*1024 }) — no timeout/killSignal. export-worker.ts:38 runs concurrency 1; worker.ts:196 exportWorker?.stop() calls worker.close() which waits for the in-flight job. grep confirms NO stop_grace_period anywhere in infra/, so Docker's default 10s grace applies and SIGKILLs the pg_dump child. processExportJob marks 'running' at export-processors.ts:24-27 and only transitions to completed/failed on return (38-48), so a killed job is left 'running' forever with no startup reaper found.
impact: On every redeploy/stop an in-progress export is hard-killed: the exportJob row dangles in 'running', a partial dump temp file leaks on the storage volume, and a genuinely hung pg_dump can never drain gracefully.
fix: Add timeout + killSignal to the pg_dump execFile; set an explicit stop_grace_period (30-60s) on the worker (and api) services exceeding worst-case in-flight job time; mark 'running' export jobs as failed on shutdown/startup.

title: Stripe client constructed with no network timeout or retry budget
description: stripe-real.driver.ts:31 this.stripe = new Stripe(env.stripeApiKey, { typescript: true }); — no timeout, no maxNetworkRetries. Stripe Node SDK default request timeout is 80s. stripe-webhook.controller.ts:98 calls await this.dispatch(event) synchronously inside the @HttpCode(200) handler (line 48); stripe-retry.job.ts:61 does the same on the sweep path.
impact: A slow/hung Stripe API ties up an Express request worker (and the webhook handler) for up to ~80s per call with no transient-error retry; during a Stripe latency event this can exhaust request concurrency, stall checkout/billing, and make the webhook slow enough that Stripe re-delivers and amplifies load. Only active once a tenant flips STRIPE_DRIVER=real (default is fake, compose:62).
fix: Pass { timeout: 10000, maxNetworkRetries: 2 } (tune) to the Stripe constructor so calls fail fast and retry transient errors with backoff.

title: Email outbox 'dead' (dead-letter) state is invisible — no metric or alert when sends are abandoned
description: email-worker.ts:147-151 sets { status: 'dead', failedAt, abandonedAt, lastError } once attempts >= maxAttempts. Worker /metrics (worker.ts:85-109) exposes only uptime + in-flight gauges — no delivered/failed/dead counter. alerts.yml has no email/queue rule. Per-job failures only hit stderr (email-worker.ts:85 console.error), which does persist via the json-file log driver (compose:76-81) but is not proactively alerted.
impact: If SMTP creds break or the provider rejects mail, every reminder/password-reset/announcement email silently dead-letters with no operator signal; first sign is a support complaint. Members miss due/overdue/hold-ready notices and password resets fail.
fix: Expose Prometheus counters for email outcomes (delivered/failed/dead) and queue depth from the worker, and alert on a non-zero rate of dead rows (or a periodic query against EmailOutbox).

title: Nightly backup never tested for restorability and silently skips remote copy if unconfigured
description: (a) Remote copy is optional: backup.sh:87 `if [ -n "$RCLONE_REMOTE" ]; then` — if unset the run still exits 0 with backups only on the same host/volume; .env.prod.example:81 ships `RCLONE_REMOTE=` blank. (b) Only integrity check is backup.sh:51 `if [ "$dump_bytes" -lt 1024 ]; then ... exit 1` — no test restore, so a structurally-corrupt/partial dump passes. (c) Wiring is manual host crontab (comment lines 13-14) with no heartbeat; infra/monitoring/alerts.yml has no backup-success alarm (only a disk-space alert at alerts.yml:54 mentioning backups in passing). No restore tooling exists: find for restore*.sh/restore*.ts returns nothing, and recovery of one library means hand-extracting one DB from a monolithic pg_dumpall (backup.sh:46-48).
impact: For a multi-tenant SaaS holding each library's whole catalogue, DR is a single un-restore-tested local dump that by default never leaves the box. A volume loss or corrupting migration can be unrecoverable, with no alert when nightly backups silently stop.
fix: Make offsite copy the default (fail loudly if RCLONE_REMOTE unset in prod), add periodic restore-verification into a throwaway DB asserting table counts, emit a backup-success heartbeat metric that alerts.yml can alarm on, and add per-tenant pg_dump/restore tooling (relocate.ts's custom-format approach) for single-library recovery.

title: read_only window lingers up to 30s after close (system-mode cache not busted on close either)
description: closeEvent() sets endedAt directly (scripts/tenant-relocate.ts:213-217 `data: { endedAt: new Date() }`) and, like openReadOnly, never busts the system-mode cache. After close, main()'s only cache work is bustResolverCache (line 154 → lines 277-278) which clears tenant:slug/sub keys, unrelated to system-mode resolution. SystemModeService.resolveTenant keeps returning the cached read_only ResolvedSystemMode until the 30s TTL expires (system-mode.service.ts:56-57, 25, 243). Same defect in scripts/storage-migrate.ts:128-129 / 183-188.
impact: After the script reports 'done' (line 159), the tenant stays in read_only — all mutations 503 — for up to an additional 30s. Degraded availability (not data loss), and makes the cutover window longer than operators expect, confusing during incident response.
fix: On close, DEL lbr:system_mode:tenant:<id> (matching SystemModeService.bust) in addition to the resolver keys so the read_only window lifts promptly across all API processes.

title: storage-migrate byte-count verification can false-fail on BSD/du-block accounting, stranding tenant in read_only
description: After `rsync -a --delete` (line 94), the script compares dirSize(from) vs dirSize(to) and throws on any inequality (lines 99-104 `if (fromSize !== toSize) throw new Error(...)`). dirSize() prefers `du -sb` (apparent bytes) but on macOS/BSD du -b is unsupported and it falls back to `du -sk` and multiplies by 1024 (lines 157-166: `const n = Number(...); return { stdout: \`${n * 1024}\t${p}\` }`), i.e. 1K allocated-block accounting, which varies with the destination filesystem's block size/allocation. So an identical-content rsync can yield fromSize !== toSize. The throw is inside the try whose catch (lines 132-135) leaves the read_only window open ('read_only window stays open for inspection'), so a false mismatch aborts and strands the tenant in read_only. Caveat: on a Linux prod host with GNU du, the -sb path is used on both sides and this won't trigger; the risk is real only on BSD/macOS or cross-FS where the fallback or block-size divergence applies — medium is appropriate.
impact: On hosts using the block-accounting fallback (macOS ops, or mixed/differing dest FS), a correct rsync is reported as failure, the migration is abandoned, and the tenant is left in read_only (mutations 503) until an operator manually clears it. Availability hit, not data loss.
fix: Verify content-equivalence independent of block allocation — e.g. an empty `rsync --dry-run --itemize-changes` after the sync, per-file size comparison (find -printf '%s'), or `rsync -c` checksums. If keeping du, require `du -sb` on both sides and fail loudly when -b is unavailable rather than silently switching to -sk units.

title: storage-migrate uses rsync --delete onto the destination path with no emptiness/identity guard — a mistyped --to-storage-url can wipe an unrelated directory
description: The destination is taken verbatim from --to-storage-url (lines 54, 65) and passed straight into `rsync -a --delete <source>/ <dest>` (line 94). There is no check that to.path is empty, newly-created, or even distinct from other tenants' storage roots — only that it differs from the source string (line 62). rsync --delete makes the destination an exact mirror of the source, deleting any pre-existing files under to.path that aren't in the source. There is also no validation that to.path is not a parent/overlapping path of from.path or of another tenant's storage directory.
impact: An operator typo in --to-storage-url (e.g. pointing at an in-use directory, a shared parent, or another tenant's storage root) causes rsync --delete to destroy whatever was already there. Combined with the source being left intact only by convention, this is a foot-gun that can delete another tenant's files.
fix: Before rsync, require the destination to either not exist or be empty (and create it), and refuse if to.path overlaps from.path or resolves under any other tenant's storage root. Consider rsync without --delete into a fresh dir, or stage into a temp dir and atomically swap.

title: Relocate has no DB-name-collision / pre-existing-destination guard before pg_restore --clean drops and overwrites
description: ensureDestinationDatabase() CREATEs the destination DB only if it doesn't already exist (scripts/tenant-relocate.ts:238-241: `if (!existing.rowCount) CREATE DATABASE`). If a database named tenant_<id> ALREADY exists on the destination host (e.g. left over from a prior failed/aborted relocate, or a name collision because dbNameForTenant only derives from tenant.id and is host-independent — scripts/_lib/cli.ts:67-69), the script proceeds to pg_restore with `--clean --if-exists` (line 127), which DROPs and recreates the existing objects in that DB. There is no check that the destination DB is empty/absent before overwriting it.
impact: If the target name is already populated on the destination host (stale data from a previous attempt, or any other DB that happens to share the tenant_<id> name), the relocate silently clobbers it via pg_restore --clean. Lower likelihood than ops-dr-1 but same class of unintended destructive write on the destination host.
fix: Before restoring, assert the destination DB is either absent or empty (e.g. zero public tables), and refuse with a clear error otherwise, forcing the operator to investigate the pre-existing DB rather than overwriting it.

title: Idempotency hash covers only the markdown body — frontmatter-only edits (title/summary/tags/sortOrder) are silently dropped on re-ingest
description: scripts/ingest-help-articles.ts:107 `const hash = createHash('sha256').update(a.body).digest('hex');` hashes only a.body. The skip guard at line 109 `if (prev && prev.sourceHash === hash && prev.archivedAt === null) { continue; }` short-circuits before the upsert. Yet title/summary/tags/sortOrder are written from frontmatter (create lines 119-122, update lines 128-131). sortOrder is derived from the filename (sortOrderFromFilename, lines 66-71). So a frontmatter-only edit (typo fix in title, summary edit, tags change, or file rename changing sortOrder) with identical body bytes leaves sourceHash unchanged → row skipped → upserted counter (line 138) not incremented → run logs upserted=0 (line 158), falsely signalling success. Confirmed tags feeds the FTS tsvector: migration 20260528170621_add_help_articles/migration.sql:86-92 adds tags to the generated search_tsv with weight 'B', so a tags-only fix also fails to update search relevance.
impact: Silent loss of help-content edits: corrected titles/summaries, retags, and re-orderings do not reach production despite a clean-looking ingest run reporting upserted=0. Especially bite-y for sortOrder (browse order) and tags (also drives FTS ranking). Blast radius is help content only — no security/billing/tenant exposure — but it is genuinely confusing and hard to diagnose because the run reports success.
fix: Hash the full raw source file bytes (frontmatter + body) rather than just a.body — thread the raw `.md` string through readArticles and hash that into sourceHash — so any frontmatter change invalidates the skip. Keep bodyMarkdown/body unchanged for rendering.

title: branding.controller writes tenant rows but never busts the resolver cache (name not affected, but pattern is fragile)
description: Confirmed branding.controller.ts:49 `controlDb.tenant.update({ where: { id: tenant.id }, data: { brandColor: color } })`, :72-75 sets brandLogoRef, :91 clears it — none call resolver.invalidate(). These columns (brandColor, brandLogoRef) are NOT in tenant-resolver.service.tenantSelect (lines 117-127: id, slug, name, defaultLocale, status, dbUrl, storageUrl, customSubdomain, tags), so there is no stale-context bug today. storage.service.ts:165 similarly updates storageUsedBytes (also not in tenantSelect) without invalidating. The invalidation contract really is implicit: only columns in tenantSelect must trigger invalidate(), and that coupling is undocumented/untested.
impact: No live correctness or cross-tenant bug — the written columns aren't cached. Genuine but low: a future edit that adds an editable column already present in tenantSelect (e.g. name, defaultLocale, customSubdomain, tags) to one of these write paths would silently serve stale TenantContext for up to 300s. Finder's confidence (0.6) and low severity are accurate.
fix: Centralize tenant-row mutation behind a helper that invalidates the resolver cache, or add a test asserting that every column in TenantResolverService.tenantSelect has a corresponding invalidate() call on its write paths. At minimum, add a comment on tenantSelect listing it as the 'cache-invalidation-triggering columns' set.

title: tenant-relocate --drop-source relies on tenants.dbUrl already pointing at the NEW home but drops the DB by deterministic name on the NEW host
description: dropSource() computes the DB to drop as dbNameForTenant(tenant.id) (line 176) and connects to it via the tenant's CURRENT dbUrl host (line 173 `const sourceUrl = tenant.dbUrl`, line 180-181 reusing that URL's host with pathname '/postgres'). After a successful relocate, tenants.dbUrl already points at the NEW host (set at line 138). Because the tenant DB name is deterministic (`tenant_<id>`) and identical on both hosts, a `--drop-source` run will DROP DATABASE on the NEW host — i.e. the live, just-migrated database — if the source and destination are the SAME Postgres host (the dev/pilot default where all tenants share one server, per provisioning service comment lines 32-34). The script's own comment at 171-173 acknowledges it drops by name computed from the id on the host derived from the (now-new) dbUrl.
impact: On a same-host relocation (the documented pilot topology: 5-20 tenants on one Postgres), running the second-phase `--drop-source` deletes the tenant's live database — total data loss for that tenant. Only safe when source and destination are physically different Postgres hosts. There is no guard verifying the host being dropped differs from the current dbUrl host.
fix: In dropSource(), require an explicit --source-host (or store the pre-relocation dbUrl in the audit row and read it back) and refuse to drop if the resolved source host+dbname equals the tenant's current dbUrl host+dbname. At minimum, abort with a loud error when source host === destination host.

title: Lockout message in tenant login leaks that an identifier exists and is currently locked
description: All other failure paths return the generic `"We couldn't sign you in with those details."` (invalidCredentials, line 180). The locked branch returns a distinct message with a countdown: `\`Too many failed attempts. Please try again in ${minutes} minute(s).\`` (lines 100-102). This branch is reached only after tenant exists+active (61-69), user exists+has hash (89-92), user active (93-96), and lockedUntil>now (97) — i.e. only for a real, active, currently-locked identifier.
impact: Account-enumeration oracle: an attacker who can trigger or observe a locked state confirms a given email/username is a valid active account on that tenant and learns the lockout duration. Limited because it requires the account to already be locked (attacker must have spent maxFailedLogins guesses, or the legit user did), but it breaks the otherwise-uniform invalid-credentials contract.
fix: Return the generic invalid-credentials message for locked accounts too (the lockout still slows the attacker without advertising the account's existence), or gate the friendly countdown behind a successful password check.

title: complete-setup lets any authenticated user reset their own password (no current-password check) with a 4-char minimum
description: POST /auth/complete-setup is gated only by `@UseGuards(AuthGuard)` (auth.controller.ts:79) — any live session. completeSetup() unconditionally sets `mustChangeCredentials: false` and, if newPassword present, a new hash, with no check that mustChangeCredentials was true and no current-password re-auth (login.service.ts:152-157). CompleteSetupDto.newPassword is `@Length(4, 200)` (dto/login.dto.ts:37) versus `@MinLength(12)` on signup (signup.dto.ts:32) and password-reset complete (password-reset.dto.ts:23). The session cookie is not re-issued after the change.
impact: Self-scoped, but: (a) a hijacked session can silently rotate the victim's password to a 4-char value without knowing the old one and with no re-auth, locking them out; (b) an owner can set a sub-policy password through this path; (c) the forced-change flag is cleared even when no password is supplied. Severity low because exploitation requires an already-compromised session.
fix: Reject the call unless mustChangeCredentials is true (or require current password for normal changes), align newPassword min length to 12, and re-issue the session cookie after a password change.

title: Secure-cookie / __Host- prefix is auto-derived from PUBLIC_APP_URL and silently downgrades over plain HTTP
description: With SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE unset (default 'auto'), `isSecure = optional('PUBLIC_APP_URL','http://localhost:3000').startsWith('https://')` (env.ts:141-144). isSecure drives both the Secure flag and the __Host-/plain cookie name for session, admin, and impersonation cookies (env.ts:172-198; cookie.service.ts:18,26; admin-cookie.service.ts:19,25,35; impersonation-cookie.service.ts:13,19,33). No `app.set('trust proxy')` and no X-Forwarded-Proto handling anywhere (grep returns nothing in main.ts/src). env.ts has no production guard forcing https.
impact: If PUBLIC_APP_URL is left at the http localhost default or configured as http while TLS terminates upstream, all auth cookies are issued without Secure and without __Host-, silently. Severity lowered to low because PUBLIC_APP_URL is also used for reset links and Stripe return URLs, so a working prod almost always has it set to the public https URL (which yields the correct isSecure=true); the downgrade requires a glaring operator misconfiguration. The gap is the absence of any hard prod safety check, not a default that breaks a correctly-configured deploy.
fix: In non-development NODE_ENV default Secure to true (require explicit opt-out) and refuse to boot in production with a non-https PUBLIC_APP_URL unless SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=true is set; trust the proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto if TLS terminates upstream.

title: MFA enrollment secret held in a process-static in-memory Map — breaks under multi-instance / restart
description: `private static readonly pending = new Map<string, string>()` (mfa.controller.ts:39). setup writes it: `MfaController.pending.set(session.sub, secret)` (line 61); verify reads it: `const secret = MfaController.pending.get(session.sub)` and throws 'No MFA setup in progress' if absent (lines 69-74). State lives only in one Node process heap.
impact: In multi-instance deployments (or after a restart between setup and verify) the verify request may land on a process with no pending entry, so admins can fail to complete enrollment. Not a secret-exposure issue (the secret is ephemeral and only persisted on successful verify), but it makes MFA onboarding flaky — and MFA is a hard prerequisite for support-key redemption.
fix: Store the pending enrollment secret in Redis with a short TTL keyed by admin id (consistent with how password-reset tokens are stored), so setup/verify work across instances and survive restarts.

title: MFA enrollment secret held in process-local memory — breaks setup/verify across multiple API instances
description: `private static readonly pending = new Map<string, string>();` (mfa.controller.ts:39). setup writes it: `MfaController.pending.set(session.sub, secret);` (mfa.controller.ts:61); verify reads it: `const secret = MfaController.pending.get(session.sub); if (!secret) throw new BadRequestException('No MFA setup in progress...')` (mfa.controller.ts:69-74). The map is process-local with no Redis/DB backing. NOTE: the current prod compose runs a single api service with no replicas/deploy-scale block (infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml api block has no `deploy.replicas`), so the cross-instance split is not triggered today; the rolling-deploy window (container recreation mid-enrollment) is the only currently-live trigger.
impact: Under horizontal scaling or a rolling redeploy, verify can land on an instance where the Map is empty, yielding 'No MFA setup in progress' for a correct code. Since MFA enrollment gates support-key redemption, an admin could be blocked from enabling MFA. Latent today (single replica) but the pattern is fragile and breaks the moment they scale out.
fix: Store the pending enrollment secret in a short-TTL Redis key (or encrypted DB column) keyed by admin id so setup and verify work regardless of which instance handles each call.

title: Support-session-log visibility check trusts the stale JWT role, not the live DB role
description: sessionLog() gates owner-wide visibility on the JWT-carried role: `if (admin.role !== 'owner' && session.adminId !== admin.sub) throw new UnauthorizedException(...)`. `admin.role` comes from AdminSessionPayload, which is stamped at login (admin-session.service.ts:13,31) and explicitly documented as 'Role at signing time. The DB row is the source of truth at request time.' Unlike AdminAuthGuard (which re-reads status/disabledAt), this check never re-reads role. An admin demoted owner→support keeps owner-level cross-admin log visibility until their token expires (adminSessionTtlSec default 3600s, env.ts:171).
impact: A demoted-to-support admin can read other admins' support session audit logs for up to ~1 hour after demotion. Read-only, narrow blast radius, self-healing at token expiry.
fix: Re-read the admin's role from controlDb.adminUser in sessionLog (or via the planned AdminRolesGuard) instead of trusting AdminSessionPayload.role.

title: Late/out-of-order invoice.payment_succeeded can resurrect a canceled subscription's status to active
description: recordPaymentSuccess unconditionally sets `status: 'active', graceUntil: null` with no guard on current status or which subscription the invoice belongs to (billing.service.ts:408-411). handleStripeInvoicePaid (lines 514-521) only maps customer→tenant and calls recordPaymentSuccess; it never reads payload.subscription. handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted (lines 497-510) sets planId=starter, status='canceled', stripeSubscriptionId=null. Stripe does not guarantee webhook ordering, so a delayed invoice.payment_succeeded arriving after subscription.deleted flips status back to 'active'.
impact: Largely benign because subscription.deleted already downgraded planId to the free starter plan, so the resurrected 'active' grants only starter entitlements. But status no longer reflects Stripe (active on a tenant with no Stripe sub), which can confuse the admin billing view (billing-admin.controller.ts:34 surfaces status) and any logic keyed on status. Risk escalates if recordPaymentSuccess is ever reused on a path that keeps a paid planId.
fix: Scope payment-success/failure handlers to the invoice's subscription (read it from its real dahlia location, see billing-6) and ignore invoices whose subscription no longer matches the local stripeSubscriptionId, or skip the status flip when stripeSubscriptionId is null / status is canceled. Treat subscription.* events as the sole authority for status.

title: ensureStripeCustomer get-or-create race can create a duplicate Stripe customer and 500 one concurrent first-time billing action
description: ensureStripeCustomer reads BillingAccount (billing.service.ts:541), and on account==null with no stripeCustomerId creates a Stripe customer over the network (line 548) then `controlDb.billingAccount.create({ data: { tenantId, ... } })` (line 560). BillingAccount.tenantId is the @id primary key (schema.prisma:485). Two concurrent first-time billing actions (double-clicked Upgrade, or checkout + portal fired together) both observe account==null, both call stripe.createCustomer (two Stripe customers created), then both attempt create — the second violates the PK and throws, surfacing as a 500. There is no upsert and no unique-violation catch.
impact: Occasional 500 on the losing request (user can retry) plus an orphaned duplicate Stripe Customer with no local mapping. Low blast radius, self-healing on retry, but leaves dangling Stripe customers and a confusing error.
fix: Upsert the BillingAccount keyed on tenantId and/or catch the unique-violation to re-read and reuse the existing stripeCustomerId. Ideally create the Stripe customer only after winning the DB row (or pass an idempotency key) so a lost race doesn't orphan a customer.

title: Signed-download secret silently falls back to the session secret in production, defeating independent rotation
description: env.ts:212 `storageSigningSecret: optional('STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET', sessionSecret),` uses optional() in ALL environments, so absent STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET the HMAC key equals sessionSecret even in prod. Contrast: sessionSecret (env.ts:136-139), adminSessionSecret (167-170), mfaMasterKey (176-184), impersonationSecret (185-188) all use required() in non-dev. The comment at env.ts:72/209-210 states the intent of an independently-rotatable secret. Cross-token replay IS blocked: SignedUrlService.verify requires `ref` as a string (signed-url.service.ts:63-70) and a session JWT has only {sub,tid,role,iat,exp} (jwt-session.service.ts:9-21, no ref), and the reverse fails because the session verify needs sub/role (jwt-session.service.ts:57-64) which the download token lacks. So the practical impact is the documented loss of rotation independence, not token confusion.
impact: Loss of intended blast-radius isolation between session auth and download authorization. An operator rotating SESSION_SECRET (e.g. after a leak) unknowingly invalidates every outstanding signed download link, and a single secret compromise affects both token classes. No direct cross-token forgery because the typed-claim guards diverge.
fix: Make STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET required() in non-development (mirror env.ts:136-139), or at minimum emit a boot warning when it falls back to sessionSecret in production.

title: Storage-quota check is a read-then-increment TOCTOU and the counter update is best-effort
description: storage.service.ts:68 `const currentBytes = await this.currentUsedBytes(tenant.id);`, line 70 `if (currentBytes + newSize > limitBytes)`, then the file is written at line 87 `const stored = await driver.put(input);`, and only afterwards lines 92-96 do `controlDb.tenant.update({ ... data: { storageUsedBytes: { increment: stored.sizeBytes } } })`, with the increment wrapped in `.catch()` (lines 97-101) that only logs a warning. Two concurrent put()s both read the same currentBytes before either increments, so both pass the check and the tenant ends up over max_storage_mb. Reachability is gated on billing: when billingEnabled is false, getEffectivePlan returns unlimitedPlan (effective-plan.service.ts:43-55, applied at 96-97) so max_storage_mb = Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER and the check never fires.
impact: When billing is enabled, a paying tenant can exceed purchased storage by up to (concurrency × per-request ceiling, 25 MB default each) under concurrent uploads. A transient counter-write failure leaves the file on disk with an under-counted counter until recomputeUsage reconciles. Low blast radius and gated on billing being on (not the documented launch default).
fix: Enforce atomically: do a conditional UPDATE (`WHERE storageUsedBytes + :n <= :limit`) first and only write the file if the row updated, compensating on driver failure; or take a per-tenant advisory lock. Surface the best-effort increment failures to monitoring, not just a warn log.

title: Non-numeric ttlSec query param produces a NaN expiry on signed URLs
description: storage-demo.controller.ts:119 `const ttlSec = ttlSecRaw ? Math.max(60, Math.min(86400, Number(ttlSecRaw))) : undefined;`. For ttlSecRaw='abc', Number('abc')=NaN, Math.min(86400,NaN)=NaN, Math.max(60,NaN)=NaN, and since ttlSecRaw is truthy the result is NaN (not undefined). In signed-url.service.ts:43 `const ttl = input.ttlSec ?? this.defaultTtlSec;` — `??` does not catch NaN, so ttl stays NaN; jwt.sign(..., { expiresIn: NaN }) (line 47) throws inside the ms library, surfacing as a 500 via the http-exception filter (handle5xx, http-exception.filter.ts).
impact: A malformed ttlSec turns a signed-url request into a 500 (re-skinned with a support code) instead of clamping to default or returning a clean 400. Affects only the caller's own request — latent robustness bug that also bypasses the intended 60..86400 clamp.
fix: Parse defensively: `const n = Number(ttlSecRaw); const ttlSec = ttlSecRaw && Number.isFinite(n) ? Math.max(60, Math.min(86400, n)) : undefined;`

title: S3Driver is an all-rejecting stub — pointing any tenant at an s3:// storage URL breaks all storage operations
description: s3-driver.ts:35-49 every method returns Promise.reject(notImplemented()) ('S3Driver is not implemented yet'). The constructor (lines 29-33) succeeds for any valid s3:// URL. The dispatcher selects it purely from the scheme: storage.service.ts:193 `if (storageUrl.startsWith('s3://')) return new S3Driver(storageUrl);`. So a tenant row with an s3:// storage_url would make every put/get/delete/stat/totalBytes throw, surfacing as opaque 500s (http-exception.filter handle5xx) and breaking recomputeUsage. BUT: provisioning hardcodes file:// (tenant-provisioning.service.ts:67 `pathToFileURL(path.join(path.resolve(this.env.storageRoot), input.tenantId)).href`) and no admin/API endpoint writes storageUrl — so today this is only reachable via a manual DB write.
impact: If an operator manually sets a tenant's storage_url to s3:// (typo or premature migration), all file features silently break for that tenant with only runtime 500s and broken images — no boot-time signal. No current code path can introduce this, so likelihood is low.
fix: Fail loudly at construction (throw 'S3 storage is not yet supported' in the S3Driver constructor) so a mis-provisioned tenant fails clearly at first use, and/or validate the storage_url scheme during provisioning to reject s3:// until the driver is implemented.

title: Custom fields written to JSONB unvalidated when the tenant has no field definitions
description: import-engine.ts:153 `if (Object.keys(customFields).length && this.fieldDefs.length)` — validation is gated on fieldDefs being non-empty. init() (import-engine.ts:117-129) leaves fieldDefs = [] when the tenant has zero defs for the entity. row-mapper.ts:169-171 lets a `custom:<key>` mapping populate customFields, and setMapping (import.service.ts:283-288) only checks FIELD_KEY_RE format, not field existence. So with no defs, customFields is written straight into JSONB (e.g. writeBook scalar.customFields, import-engine.ts:315). dynamic-validator.ts:68-77 confirms that calling validateRecord with empty defs + unknownFields:'reject' would reject every supplied key — so the guard is what causes the gap.
impact: Importing into a tenant that has defined no custom fields silently accepts arbitrary custom-field keys (typos/junk) into JSONB that the manual editor (unknownFields:'reject') would reject — inconsistent with the rest of the app and orphaned data invisible in the UI. Not a memory/cross-tenant issue: FIELD_KEY_RE constrains keys to ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{1,49}$ so no __proto__/prototype pollution.
fix: Run validateRecord whenever customFields is non-empty, dropping the `&& this.fieldDefs.length` condition: with empty defs and unknownFields:'reject' it correctly turns every supplied custom key into a clear per-row error instead of writing junk.

title: Numeric transforms silently coerce malformed input instead of rejecting it
description: transforms.ts:25 `const cleaned = raw.trim().replace(/[^0-9-]/g, '');` then :27 `Number.parseInt(cleaned, 10)`. '5-7' → cleaned '5-7' → parseInt = 5; '1-800' → 1; '12 copies' → '12' → 12. No rejection of embedded non-numeric content. Neither toInt nor toMoneyCents (transforms.ts:58-87) bounds magnitude; toMoneyCents('25000000') → no decimal sep → cents = Math.round(25000000*100) = 2,500,000,000, which exceeds Postgres int4 max 2,147,483,647. Target columns are all Int: schema.prisma:431 amountCents, :291 priceCents, :228 numPages, :365 renewedCount. The oversized value reaches the DB and fails as a generic db_error (dbIssue fallback, import-engine.ts:92) rather than an actionable validation message.
impact: Garbage-but-parseable numeric cells are silently turned into plausible wrong values (page-range '5-7' stored as numPages 5) — silent data corruption during migration. Oversized money/int values surface as an opaque per-row 'db_error' instead of 'value out of range'.
fix: In toInt, reject input that contains non-numeric, non-leading-sign characters (test /^-?\d+$/ after stripping only grouping separators). In toInt/toMoneyCents, fail with a precise reason when the result exceeds 2,147,483,647 so the librarian gets an out-of-range message instead of a raw DB error.

title: errors.csv export does not neutralize spreadsheet-formula-leading cells (CSV injection)
description: import.service.ts:383-386 `function csvCell(value: string)` only does RFC-4180 quoting: `if (/[",\r\n]/.test(value)) return \`"${value.replace(/"/g, '""')}"\`; return value;` — no = + - @ neutralization. The message column originates from uploaded content: row-mapper.ts:191 ``${def.label}: ${result.reason}.`` and transform reasons embed the raw cell, e.g. transforms.ts:48 `not a yes/no value: "${raw}"`, transforms.ts:178 `not a valid ISBN-13: "${raw}"`, transforms.ts:147 `unrecognized date: "${raw}"`. errorsCsv (import.service.ts:199-212) writes these via csvCell into import-errors.csv (download headers at import.controller.ts:134-137).
impact: A crafted cell like `=HYPERLINK(...)` or `=cmd|...` echoes through an invalid_value error message into the downloaded import-errors.csv and executes as a formula when a staff admin opens it in Excel/LibreOffice — classic CSV/formula injection against the reviewer. Blast radius limited (requires opening in a spreadsheet and dismissing the macro warning), hence low.
fix: In csvCell, prefix any value whose first character is = + - @ (or tab/CR) with a single quote or space before the RFC-4180 quoting, since these are end-user-opened spreadsheet downloads.

title: Loan import flips copy to on_loan regardless of prior status (resurrects lost/damaged/withdrawn copies)
description: commitLoan resolves the copy purely by barcode (findCopyByBarcode, import-engine.ts:709-717, which only filters archivedAt) and then, for status 'active', unconditionally runs `await tx.bookCopy.update({ where: { id: copyId }, data: { status: 'on_loan' } })` (import-engine.ts:525) with no check on the copy's current status. The manual checkout path rejects when `copy.status !== expectedCopyStatus` (loans.service.ts:210-217) and uses a guarded `bookCopy.updateMany({ where: { id, status: expectedCopyStatus } })` (loans.service.ts:289-297). Unlike the duplicate-active-loan case (blocked by the loans_one_active_per_copy partial unique index), there is NO DB constraint on the copy's status field, so importing an active loan onto a copy currently lost/damaged/withdrawn/reserved silently overwrites its status to on_loan. (The duplicate-active-loan path is safe — see import-1 verdict.)
impact: A migration that imports open loans can silently resurrect a lost/damaged/withdrawn copy to on_loan, masking that the copy is actually missing or out of circulation. Narrower than the claimed duplicate-loan corruption, but a real availability/inventory inconsistency.
fix: In commitLoan, for status 'active' read the copy's current status and either reject (row error) when it is not 'available', or flip with a conditional `bookCopy.updateMany({ where: { id: copyId, status: 'available' }, data: { status: 'on_loan' } })` and treat count===0 as a row-level conflict, mirroring loans.service.ts:289-297.

title: Expired exports remain downloadable until the hourly cleanup cron runs
description: streamExport() gates only on `job.status !== 'completed' || !job.filePath` (export-download.ts:9) and fs.access (line 13) — it never reads job.expiresAt. The lazy purge runs hourly: registry.ts:46-49 `{ name: 'export-file-cleanup', intervalMs: 60 * 60_000 }`. TTL is 24h (export.constants.ts:8 `EXPORT_TTL_HOURS = 24`; export.service.ts:30-32 stamps expiresAt). export-cleanup.job.ts:28-32 only nulls filePath/fileBytes when expiresAt < now, so until that hourly sweep runs both the on-disk file and the filePath column persist past expiry and res.download() (export-download.ts:19) serves it. publicExportJob exposes expiresAt to clients (export.service.ts:22) but the read path doesn't enforce it.
impact: For up to ~1h after the 24h TTL lapses, the full-DB export (all tenant member PII, or for admin scope the control DB + every tenant DB) stays retrievable past its stated expiry. Blast radius is bounded: still ownership-scoped (tenant-export.controller.ts:63-65 checks targetTenantId; admin path requires AdminAuthGuard) and the window is capped by the cron. Real but low — it weakens the documented retention promise rather than enabling a new principal to read data.
fix: In streamExport(), also reject when `job.expiresAt != null && job.expiresAt < new Date()` with the same NotFoundException, so expiry is enforced on read regardless of cron timing.

title: Generic table reader interpolates table names but does not escape embedded double-quotes in identifiers
description: Line 213: `const res = await client.query(\`SELECT * FROM "${name}"\`);` — the identifier is wrapped in double quotes but embedded " characters are not doubled. `name` comes from pg_tables WHERE schemaname='public' (lines 205-210), i.e. the Prisma-generated schema, not user input. So it is not exploitable today; it is a latent identifier-quoting hazard on a generic reader used for tenant, control, AND 'all' scopes.
impact: No exploit today (table names are developer/migration-controlled). A future migration or control-DB table whose name contained a quote would break the query or, with a maliciously crafted name, run unintended SQL. Defense-in-depth gap on a path that runs against every DB including the control plane.
fix: Double embedded quotes: `SELECT * FROM "${name.replace(/"/g, '""')}"`, or use a pg identifier-quoting helper. Cheap, removes the latent hazard.

title: Admin export 'all' / 'control' download has no ownership/authorization scoping beyond AdminAuthGuard — but more importantly the admin download endpoint returns ANY job, including another principal's, with only AdminAuthGuard
description: The admin download handler `download(@Param('id') id, @Res() res)` calls `this.svc.get(id)` (which only checks existence) and streams it with no further scoping — any authenticated platform admin can download any export job by id, including ones requested by a different admin (requestedById is never checked). This is acceptable IF all platform admins are equally trusted to read the full control + all-tenant export, which is the design intent here (the 'all'/'control' scopes already expose everything to any admin). Noting it as low/info: it is not a privilege boundary violation within the admin tier, but it means there is no per-admin attribution enforcement on the most sensitive artifact in the system (the all-tenant dump). If the admin role is ever subdivided (e.g. read-only support admins), this endpoint would over-share.
impact: Within the current single-tier admin model, no cross-principal leak (all admins may read everything). Becomes a real authorization gap the moment admin roles are differentiated. Low today.
fix: If admin roles stay flat, document the intent. If/when roles are subdivided, scope the download to requestedById or to an explicit role capability.

title: Web /api/metrics endpoint is unauthenticated
description: apps/web/app/api/metrics/route.ts:13 `export function GET() {` has zero auth: it returns `libriant_web_uptime_seconds` and `libriant_web_build_info{node_env="${process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development'}"} 1` (line 21) to any caller. There is no middleware (confirmed: `find apps/web -name middleware.ts` returns nothing; the only gating in the app is the `currentSession`/`currentAdminSession` checks inside page layouts, which do not cover app/api/* route handlers). Contrast with apps/web/app/[locale]/admin/(authed)/layout.tsx:23-24 which calls `currentAdminSession()` and redirects. So /api/metrics is reachable unauthenticated, exactly as described.
impact: Minor info disclosure: an unauthenticated visitor learns web process uptime and the NODE_ENV string. No tenant data, secrets, or per-request metrics are exposed today, so blast radius is small. The real risk is forward-looking: the route's own comment (lines 4-6) says 'richer metrics (request counters, error rates) land later'; if those are added to this same open handler, the endpoint silently becomes an operational-data-leak surface.
fix: Gate the route behind a bearer token compared against an env secret (e.g. METRICS_TOKEN) or restrict it to the internal network / a non-public port so only the Prometheus scraper reaches it. At minimum add the guard now, before richer metrics are added.

title: TenantProvisioningService.teardown() drops a DB by name with no internal liveness guard
description: teardown() drops purely by name: line 94 `await admin.query(`DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS "${dbName}"`)` with dbName = dbNameFor(tenantId), no check the tenant is archived/orphaned. It IS already wired to a live-tenant deletion: admin-tenants.controller.ts:168 `await this.provisioning.teardown(tenant.id)`. But that controller is @UseGuards(AdminAuthGuard) (line 35), and remove() requires a typed-slug confirmation before dropping (lines 161-163: `if (dto.confirmSlug.trim().toLowerCase() !== tenant.slug.toLowerCase()) throw new BadRequestException(...)`), and is documented as 'IRREVERSIBLE — owner break-glass' (139-147). So the dangerous capability is intentional and guarded at the real call site; teardown() lacking its own guard is defense-in-depth only.
impact: If a new caller is added that passes a live tenant id without the controller's typed-confirmation guard, it would irrecoverably drop that tenant's DB. No such caller exists today; all current callers either pass a fresh signup-rollback id or go through the confirmed admin-delete path. Low/defense-in-depth.
fix: Add a defensive `force`/`confirm` flag to teardown() and/or assert the tenant row is absent or status='archived' before DROP, so the method is safe regardless of caller. Optionally rename-then-drop-on-delay for a recovery window.

title: migrateDeploy() parses human-readable Prisma stdout to count applied migrations; brittle and inconsistent across code paths
description: migrateDeploy() line 297: `const applied = (out.match(/└─|have been applied/gi) ?? []).length;` — the alternation matches BOTH the tree glyph and the summary phrase, so a single applied migration can be counted twice (one tree branch + the 'have been applied' header). scripts/tenant-migrate.ts:138 uses a different regex for the same purpose: `(out.match(/└─\s*\d+/g) ?? []).length`, so the two paths disagree on what 'N applied' means. The migration itself is driven by Prisma; this only affects the summary string returned in MaintenanceTargetResult / CLI output.
impact: Operators see inaccurate 'N migration(s) applied' counts in the admin maintenance panel and CLI, which can mask a partial or no-op fleet migration. Reporting-only — no data corruption.
fix: Stop parsing stdout. Use `prisma migrate status` or query _prisma_migrations to determine applied/pending counts, and share one helper between maintenance-processors.ts and scripts/tenant-migrate.ts.

title: Relocate/storage-migrate attribute the read_only window to an arbitrary 'first owner admin', not the operator
description: firstOwnerAdminId() (tenant-relocate.ts:220-227, storage-migrate.ts:190-197): `controlDb.adminUser.findFirst({ where: { role: 'owner', status: 'active' } })` then used as createdByAdminId on the read_only SystemModeEvent (openReadOnly, tenant-relocate.ts:201-210 / storage-migrate.ts:170-180). The createdByAdminId column is required (schema.prisma:959) and non-null, and the relation onDelete: Restrict. The accompanying auditEvent is written with actorType:'system' (tenant-relocate.ts:142-150, storage-migrate.ts:112-122), so there is no field anywhere recording which human ran the command.
impact: A customer-visible, destructive operation (read-only + data move) is attributed to whichever owner admin sorts first, defeating accountability. Minor for a small ops team but relevant to the SOC2/GDPR posture.
fix: Require a --by-admin=<email|id> argument validated against adminUser and stamp it on the SystemModeEvent.createdByAdminId and as actorId on the audit event.

title: Admin hard-delete of a tenant does NOT open a read_only/maintenance window before dropping the live DB — concurrent requests race the DROP
description: remove() drops the live tenant DB (line 168 `await this.provisioning.teardown(tenant.id)`) without first putting the tenant into read_only/maintenance mode. teardown() runs pg_terminate_backend then DROP DATABASE (tenant-provisioning.service.ts:88-94). Any in-flight tenant request whose Prisma pool is mid-query gets its backend killed and the DB dropped underneath it; the control-plane Tenant row is only deleted afterward (line 176), so the TenantResolver Redis cache and warm tenant Prisma pools can still route new requests to a database that has just been destroyed until the cache/pool turns over. This is a hard-delete break-glass op so blast radius is bounded to the tenant being deleted (which is intended to go away), hence low — but it can surface as confusing 500s rather than a clean 503 during the delete window.
impact: During an admin hard-delete, concurrent requests for that tenant hit a dropped/terminated database and surface as raw 500s / connection errors instead of a clean maintenance 503, and may briefly route to a non-existent DB via stale resolver cache. Bounded to the tenant being deleted.
fix: Open a tenant-scoped maintenance SystemModeEvent (or set status='archived' and bust the resolver cache) before calling teardown(), so in-flight and new requests get a clean 503 and the pool is drained before the DROP.

title: STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET silently falls back to the session secret; compose uses a non-failing guard unlike its peers
description: env.ts:212 `storageSigningSecret: optional('STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET', sessionSecret),` — reuses the JWT session secret if unset, in all environments. docker-compose.prod.yml:50 `STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET: ${STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET:-}` (empty default) whereas peers at lines 46-49 use `${VAR:?...}` (SESSION_SECRET/ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET/IMPERSONATION_SECRET/MFA_MASTER_KEY all abort compose up if unset). Consumed at apps/api/src/storage/signed-url.service.ts:30 `this.secret = env.storageSigningSecret;`. Happy path is safe: ensure-env.sh has `ensure_rand STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET 32`, so the auto-deploy always generates it.
impact: Defense-in-depth gap only. A hand-edited/partial .env.prod that omits STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET boots silently with the storage HMAC keyed to the session secret, coupling two secrets meant to rotate independently (rotating SESSION_SECRET would then also invalidate all outstanding signed download URLs). Not exploitable on the standard deploy path.
fix: Make compose fail-fast: change line 50 to `STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET: ${STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET:?STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET is required}` to match its peers; optionally require() it in env.ts for non-dev instead of falling back to sessionSecret.

title: Numeric env vars are parsed with Number(...) and no NaN/finite validation
description: Every numeric field is `Number(optional('KEY','default'))` with no Number.isFinite/isNaN guard anywhere in env.ts. I tested the two specific consumers the finder called out: (1) tenantClientCacheSize feeds `new LRUCache({ max: env.tenantClientCacheSize })` (tenant-prisma.service.ts:38) and `new LRUCache({max: NaN})` THROWS 'max option must be a nonnegative integer' — i.e. a NaN cache size FAILS LOUD at boot, it does not silently misbehave. (2) bcryptCost feeds password.service.ts:20/23; `bcrypt.hashSync('x', NaN)` returns a valid `$2b$10$...` hash (bcryptjs falls back to cost 10) — it neither throws nor produces a trivially weak hash, just cost 10 instead of 12.
impact: A typo'd numeric env var violates env.ts's stated 'present + valid, or boot fails loudly' contract. Real but limited: NaN cache size crashes boot (loud), NaN bcryptCost silently uses cost 10 (mild). The sharp silent case (upload ceiling disabled) is its own finding below.
fix: Add a `requiredNumber(key, fallback)` helper that throws on `!Number.isFinite(n)` (and rejects negatives where nonsensical) and use it for all numeric fields, restoring the file's fail-loud guarantee.

title: controlDbUrl and pgSuperuserUrl have hardcoded localhost-with-default-credentials fallbacks and no production guard
description: controlDbUrl: `optional('CONTROL_DATABASE_URL', 'postgresql://libriant:libriant@localhost:5432/libriant_control')` (149-152) and pgSuperuserUrl: `optional('PG_SUPERUSER_URL', 'postgresql://libriant:libriant@localhost:5432/libriant_control')` (205-208) — both plain optional() with embedded `libriant:libriant` creds, no `nodeEnv !== 'development'` gate, unlike sessionSecret/adminSessionSecret/mfaMasterKey/impersonationSecret which require() in non-dev. docker-compose.prod.yml:36 and :71 always set these from POSTGRES_PASSWORD, so the standard deploy is safe.
impact: Defense-in-depth gap: a prod process started with these vars unset (outside compose) silently connects to localhost Postgres with well-known libriant/libriant creds instead of refusing to boot. pgSuperuserUrl is the role used to CREATE DATABASE during tenant provisioning. Also documents the dev superuser password in source. Not exploitable on the standard compose deploy.
fix: require() controlDbUrl and pgSuperuserUrl when nodeEnv !== 'development', matching the secret handling, so an unset DB URL in prod aborts boot.

title: NaN STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES silently DISABLES the per-request upload size limit (no error)
description: env.ts:214 `storageMaxUploadBytes: Number(optional('STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES', String(25 * 1024 * 1024)))` with no finite check. This value is passed directly as multer's fileSize limit at branding.controller.ts:55, catalog/covers.controller.ts:39, storage/storage-demo.controller.ts:58, and members/photos.controller.ts:39 — all `FileInterceptor('file', { limits: { fileSize: loadEnv().storageMaxUploadBytes } })`. Multer enforces the limit via `bytesWritten > limits.fileSize`. I verified that `200 > NaN` is `false` and `NaN > anything` is `false`, so when STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES is malformed (e.g. a stray char, `STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES=25mb`) the value becomes NaN and the size comparison is ALWAYS false — multer never rejects a file for being too large. Unlike the LRU cache (which throws on NaN at boot) and bcrypt (which falls back to cost 10), this one fails OPEN and silently: the app boots fine and the upload ceiling is gone. This is the genuinely silent+harmful instance the config-2 finding buried among many fields. Happy-path safe (compose does not set this var, so the '25MB' default applies; only an operator typo triggers it).
impact: A malformed STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES removes the hard per-request upload ceiling across every file-upload endpoint (cover images, member photos, branding logos), enabling unbounded uploads — disk-fill / DoS and per-plan quota bypass — with no boot error or log to indicate the limit is off.
fix: Parse with a requiredNumber helper that throws on !Number.isFinite(n) (and rejects <= 0), so a malformed upload ceiling aborts boot instead of silently disabling enforcement.

title: Reservation-expiry cron promotes a hold but never rebalances the remaining queue positions
description: The cron promotion sets `next.queuePosition = null` (line 140) but issues NO `UPDATE reservations SET queuePosition = queuePosition - 1` afterward — queuePosition appears in the file only at lines 104, 118, 140 (grep-confirmed). Both service paths DO run the cascade rebalance: reservations.service.ts:515-521 and loans.service.ts:412-418 (`... queuePosition - 1 WHERE status='queued' AND queuePosition > 0`). The CHECK `reservations_queue_position_when_queued` (migration:530-534) requires queuePosition >= 1 for queued, which positions 2,3 still satisfy, so no constraint is violated.
impact: After an expiry-driven promotion the queue keeps a hole (remaining holds at positions 2,3 with no 1) until the next service-path promotion heals it (its `queuePosition > 0` rebalance). Cosmetic/ordering only — list view orders by queuePosition asc so displayed line numbers are off-by-one, but the next-in-line is still correctly the lowest position. No data loss.
fix: After the promotion update, run the same `queuePosition = queuePosition - 1 WHERE bookId=... AND status='queued' AND queuePosition > 0` rebalance the service paths use.

title: Per-member active-loans cap is checked before the transaction and can be exceeded by concurrent checkouts
description: The cap check reads `const activeCount = await client.loan.count({ where: { memberId: input.memberId, status: 'active' } })` and compares to `settings.maxActiveLoans` at lines 174-183 — entirely BEFORE `client.$transaction(...)` which starts at line 224. The count is never re-evaluated inside the tx, and no per-member loan constraint exists (the only loan partial unique index is per-copy: migration:458-460 `loans_one_active_per_copy ON loans(copyId) WHERE returnedAt IS NULL`).
impact: Two checkouts of two different copies for an at-limit member, processed concurrently from two stations, both pass the pre-check and both commit, putting the member one (or more) over maxActiveLoans. Pure policy bypass at the exact boundary — no row corruption, limited blast radius.
fix: Re-count active loans inside the transaction after a pg_advisory_xact_lock on the member id (the lock pattern already exists in placeHold) and abort if over cap; or accept and document the small over-count.

title: Misleading duplicate-error message: member email is not actually unique
description: members.service.ts:447-448 maps any unique violation to 'A member with this number (or email) already exists.' The only unique constraint on members is migration 20260526184041_init/migration.sql:475-477 `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "members_member_number_unique_active" ON "members"("memberNumber") WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL`. Email is non-unique: migration line 329 `CREATE INDEX "members_email_idx" ON "members"("email")` and schema.prisma:347 `@@index([email])` (column is `email String? @db.Citext`, schema.prisma:321). No path raises a P2002 on email, so the '(or email)' clause is dead/misleading.
impact: Cosmetic but misleading error text implying email is enforced unique when duplicate-email members are silently accepted. If unique email per library was intended, this is a silent gap; otherwise purely cosmetic.
fix: Drop the '(or email)' clause to match reality, OR add a partial unique index on email-among-active members if duplicates should be rejected. Decide intentionally (families share emails).

title: Unbounded growth of members.staffNotes via repeated status changes
description: members.service.ts:376-384 builds `noteAddition = `\n[${new Date().toISOString()}] status → ${input.status}: ${input.reason.trim()}`` and writes `staffNotes: noteAddition ? (existing.staffNotes ?? '') + noteAddition : undefined` — pure append, never truncated. Column is `staffNotes String?` with no length cap (schema.prisma:334) and is returned in MemberDto (toDto, members.service.ts:508 `staffNotes: row.staffNotes`). Per-call reason is DTO-capped but the cumulative column is not.
impact: Repeated active↔suspended toggles grow staffNotes without bound, bloating row size, list/get payloads, and audit before/after snapshots. Low blast radius, slow data-bloat.
fix: Record status-change history in the audit log (already done via audit.record at members.service.ts:387) instead of concatenating into staffNotes, or cap/rotate the appended notes and add a DB length limit.

title: Archiving a book is allowed while its copies are still on loan (no open-business check, unlike members)
description: books.service.ts:347-349 `if (input.archived !== undefined) { data.archivedAt = input.archived ? new Date() : null; }` — no check for outstanding loans on the book's copies, in contrast to members.service.ts:411-424 which refuses archive with open loans/holds. Default catalog list hides archived (books.service.ts where.archivedAt = null, per lane brief line ~85). So a book with on_loan copies can be archived and hidden while the physical copy is still out.
impact: Inconsistent view: title hidden from catalog while a copy is still circulating and must be returned. Loan/copy rows are untouched and the book is restorable, so low severity, but it can confuse return/reporting flows.
fix: Mirror the member-archive safety check: refuse to archive a book that has any copy with status on_loan (or any open loan against its copies), or surface a warning. Confirm intended behavior with product.

title: support-session-expiry can mark a session ended but never send the notification if the worker dies mid-tick
description: support-session-expiry.job.ts:33-37 `updateMany({ where: { id: s.id, endedAt: null }, data: { endedAt: now, endedReason: 'expired' } })` then, only after `if (update.count === 0) continue;`, lines 39-44 `await notifs.sessionEnded({...})`. Two separate non-transactional operations. The re-sweep query (lines 23-26) filters `endedAt: null`, so once endedAt is set the session is never re-found. The idempotency key support.session.ended:<id> guards duplicates, not omission.
impact: If the worker crashes / BullMQ stalls the job between the DB flip (line 33) and the enqueue (line 39), the sessionEnded notification is permanently lost — the next sweep skips the session because endedAt is now set. True at-least-once gap, but narrow window and low blast radius (a support session ends with no notice; no money/tenant-data impact).
fix: Enqueue the email within the same logical unit as the status flip, or have the notifier query 'ended-but-not-notified' (add a notifiedAt column) so a re-sweep can recover. Low priority vs the fine/hold issues.

title: reservation-expiry sweep does not rebalance queuePosition after promotion — diverges from service, queue positions drift
description: reservation-expiry.job.ts:134-148 sets only the promoted row's queuePosition to null (line 140); there is no cascade UPDATE decrementing the remaining queued reservations. The canonical path does: reservations.service.ts:515-521 `UPDATE reservations SET "queuePosition" = "queuePosition" - 1, "updatedAt" = NOW() WHERE "bookId"=... AND status='queued' AND "queuePosition" > 0`. The spec (reservation-expiry.job.spec.ts) never asserts position rebalancing. migration.sql:530-534 (reservations_queue_position_when_queued) still passes with stale positions (>=1), so no crash.
impact: After a sweep promotion, everyone behind keeps a now-off-by-one queuePosition. Ordering is preserved (next promotion still picks lowest position), but positions shown to patrons are stale relative to the service path, and any logic assuming contiguous positions is wrong. Cosmetic-to-minor; no data loss.
fix: Mirror the queuePosition-decrement cascade from promoteNextHoldInTx (reservations.service.ts:515-521) inside the inline sweep, and add a spec assertion to keep the two implementations in sync.

title: Scheduled-jobs runner sets no per-tenant timeout/lock; a slow tenant DB can stall a 60s cron past its next interval with no dedup protection beyond BullMQ default
description: The reservation-pickup-expiry and announcement-publish jobs run every 60_000ms (registry.ts:29-31, 51-54) and iterate every active tenant serially opening a Prisma client each (reservation-expiry.job.ts:52-62). The worker has concurrency:4 (scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:95) and the repeatable job carries no lockDuration/timeout override. If one tenant's DB is slow, a single tick can exceed 60s; BullMQ's repeat scheduler will enqueue the next occurrence, and with concurrency 4 a backlog of overlapping ticks of the SAME job can run concurrently against the same tenants. Because the sweeps' writes are guarded by updateMany status-predicates (e.g. reservation-expiry.job.ts:102-106), overlap is mostly safe, but it amplifies the queue-2 copy-claim race and multiplies tenant Prisma connections under the LRU cap.
impact: Under a slow tenant, overlapping identical cron ticks increase connection pressure (TenantPrismaService LRU, default ~50 hot clients) and widen the window for the unguarded copy-claim in queue-2. No correctness break on its own given the status guards, but a reliability amplifier. Low.
fix: Give long-iterating repeatable jobs a stable jobId or a per-job Redis lock so a new tick is skipped while the previous one is still running, and/or cap the per-tenant work with a statement timeout.

title: Web readyz fetch to the API has no timeout — probe can hang on a slow API
description: readyz/route.ts:17 const res = await fetch(`${apiBase.replace(/\/$/, '')}/readyz`, { cache: 'no-store' }); — no AbortController/AbortSignal.timeout. undici has no short default request timeout.
impact: A reachable-but-slow API makes the web readiness probe hang and tie up a Next.js server worker per probe until the socket closes; the Compose healthcheck (wget timeout 5s, compose:202-207) still marks web unhealthy, so blast radius is small. Severity medium->low: probe resource hygiene, not an availability gap.
fix: Wrap the fetch in AbortSignal.timeout(3000) so the probe returns 503 with reachable:false promptly.

title: No unhandledRejection / uncaughtException guards in API or worker process
description: grep -rn 'unhandledRejection|uncaughtException' apps/api/src apps/web returns NONE. main.ts only catches the bootstrap promise (main.ts:48-51). worker.ts:209-210 only registers SIGTERM/SIGINT. Detached paths cited by the finder ARE individually guarded: tenant-prisma.service.ts:44-53 dispose has .catch at :48; support-audit.interceptor.ts:23-28 detaches via rxjs tap but has try/catch at :42-53.
impact: An unhandled rejection in some future/untracked detached path terminates the process abruptly without draining in-flight work or emitting a structured fatal log, making it poorly observable. Downgraded medium->low because every detached path the finder cited is already guarded; this is defensive hardening, not a known live bug.
fix: Install process-level unhandledRejection/uncaughtException handlers in main.ts and worker.ts that log a structured fatal record and exit non-zero for a clean orchestrator restart.

title: No alert for the worker being down or for any background-job failure
description: alerts.yml:12-18 TargetDown: up == 0 for 2m covers ANY target including libriant-worker. No rule references Redis memory (API exposes libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes at health.controller.ts:133-141 but no alert), no scheduled-job-staleness rule (scheduledLastResults at worker.ts:67 is not even a metric), and prometheus.yml:17-21 leaves the alerting/alertmanagers block commented out so NO rule is delivered.
impact: Worker death IS detected by TargetDown but, with Alertmanager unconfigured, nothing is delivered — all rules (incl. critical API-down, disk-critical, PG-connections-critical) are display-only. Redis memory pressure and silent job-stall (process stays up) have no rule at all. Downgraded medium->low: the headline 'worker has no down alert' is a false positive; the real gaps are un-wired Alertmanager and missing Redis/staleness rules.
fix: Wire a real Alertmanager target in prometheus.yml; add a Redis-memory alert on libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes vs a maxmemory gauge; add a scheduled-job-staleness alert; optionally a dedicated LibriantWorkerDown for clarity.

title: Worker boot failures degrade silently — failed sub-worker stays 'starting' but process keeps running
description: worker.ts:123-173 each sub-worker boots via startXxx().then(h=>handle=h).catch(err=>console.error(...)). readyz at worker.ts:76 gates ONLY on emailWorker && scheduledJobs && importWorker — it omits maintenanceWorker and exportWorker. So an export/maintenance boot failure leaves its handle null, /healthz reports that queue 'starting' forever (worker.ts:64-65), readyz stays 200, process keeps serving. Only a single stderr line (e.g. worker.ts:172) records it.
impact: A partial worker boot (e.g. export worker can't connect) is invisible to readiness and monitoring; export/maintenance jobs queue and never run, with one easily-lost console.error as the only signal. Low severity: a selective partial boot is rare since all sub-workers share the same Redis.
fix: Include all required sub-workers in the readyz gate (or fail the whole process if a required one can't start), and expose per-queue boot state as a metric.

title: Stripe-retry sweep: comment claims it clears errors on unknown types but the default branch does not
description: stripe-retry.job.ts:36-41 selects error IS NOT NULL AND processedAt IS NULL. dispatch() default branch (104-106) comment says 'Unknown type — clear the error so it doesn't loop forever' then just returns — it neither clears error nor sets processedAt. Persistence happens only in the caller's success path (62-65), which runs for every non-throwing dispatch (incl. default), so today an unknown errored event IS marked processed. The comment misrepresents where the guarantee lives.
impact: Benign today (caller clears it). Latent: if dispatch is ever refactored to own its persistence, an unknown errored event would re-select every 50-row tick forever. Comment is actively misleading.
